ELLIOTT (Ivindersley): Mr. Speaker, while I have no great demand from my constituency for a national flag, the people perhaps being more interested at the present time in difficulties of a personal nature, being situated in the drought area, I feel that the subject is interesting from an informative point of view.
When one is contemplating a national flag he is likely to be influenced by conflicting emotions. He may desire the retention of the union jack because of British alliances, and because it is symbolic of the many historical events in the process of building the British Empire. There seems to be a considerable amount of confusion about our flags in the minds of Canadian people, and while the National Anthem creates a reverence for British monarchy and institutions, the singing of "O Canada" stimulates the joy of everything purely Canadian.
I am thinking at the moment of the people of many different nationalities comprising Canadian nationhood who immigrated to Canada for a purpose. The object prompting such a move was doubtless the desire to secure an improvement in their standard of living and, believing Canada afforded that opportunity, after much deliberation they decided to take the momentous step. I can almost feel the tumult of emotions that struggled for predominance in the breasts of these many individuals before deciding the most uncertain action of their lives. They had to decide whether to hold steadfast to their old traditions and institutions, or set their eyes on a new star, trusting-and in human life how very important that quality is. They were anxious to contribute their efforts, be they large or small, to the moulding of a new nation. The young men and women
born in Canada, who are not moved by the same sentiments as previous generations with regard to old world institutions and the symbols that represent their struggle for emancipation, look for emblems depicting more particular!}' Canadian history, while still retaining possibly a symbol of our progenitors, as does the Canadian coat of arms.
The red ensign of the British merchant marine ships, with the Canadian coat of arms in the fly, after floating for thirty years over every dominion public building in Canada was displaced, and the union jack restored.
The shield on Canadian marine flags goes back to the very dawn of our official flag. In order to place a description on the record for those who may read the report of the debate, may I state that in the upper left hand canton are depicted the three golden lions of Normandy, brought from the ancient French province of Normandy by William the Conqueror, and first inscribed on our flag by Richard I of England. In the upper right hand canton we have the lion of Scotland. In the centre cantons we have the harp of Ireland, and also the fleur-de-lis first placed on the British flag by Edward III, in honour of the French princess who was his mother. Beneath these four cantons we have three maple leaves representing Canada. This is placed on the fly of each of the two marine flags of Canada. At present Canada's only flag is the red ensign. In 1892, the dominion government passed a regulation allowing the arms of Canada to be placed on the red ensign for mercantile purposes. The fact that there is no legal right, so far as I know, to fly this flag on land, may account for the change to the union jack a few years ago.
I heartily agree with the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) who advocates the adoption of a national flag for Canada, the importance of which he has brought to our attention. It is of interest, however, to know that Canada already has a flag which is 176 years older than the union jack or, as correctly described, the union flag. When I say Canada has a flag, I refer to the flag of Nova Scotia, a part of Canada, although it is conceded that she did not want to be. I am pleased to see a number of representatives from Nova Scotia in the house.
It is a matter of record that in 1625 Charles I of England granted to Nova Scotia a coat-of- arms and a flag with an orange tawny field. This flag, as I have said, is 176 years older than the union jack. The circumstances in connection with the making of it take us back to the days of Queen Anne. We find that after the Treaty of Union was signed
A Canadian Flag

between England and Scotland on January 16, 1707.	Queen Anne was requested to
appoint ensigns armorial to conjoin into one flag, the crosses of St. George and St. Andrew, and in May, 1707, the flag was displayed at St. Paul's Cathedral in London, where a solemn celebration was held to commemorate the union.
It was not, however, until 1S01, when Ireland was joined in the legislative union that the cross of St. Patrick was added. The result of this addition is the union jack or union flag in use to-day by Great Britain and all her colonies.
It may not be a bad idea for the house humbly to pray the province of Nova Scotia for the privilege of flying this as the national flag of Canada. In the centre of the blue cross of St. Andrew, on the flag of Nova Scotia, we find a red lion, all of which is placed on an orange tawny field. This is a very attractive flag indeed, and one no doubt of which Nova Scotia is proud.
We have adopted the beaver as a national emblem. We find it was first used in 1630 by Sir William Alexander, who received in 1621 a grant to colonize Nova Scotia from King James I of England, who was also King James VI of Scotland. So far as I know, no objection has been raised by Nova Scotia to the use of the beaver as an emblem. Therefore I feel confident that Nova Scotia would not refuse us the use of her ancient flag.
New Zealand, Australia, and South Africa have flags of their own. I can remember how anxious we were at one time to take part in the conflict in South Africa. Recently there has come to my notice an article from a Vancouver paper dealing with the flag of South Africa. Dated at Vancouver, September 27, 1937, the article states:
When the team of forty-three South African lawn bowlers arrived on the Pacific coast during their trans-Canada tour, they were determined to include a pilgrimage to a tree stump at Campbell river, Vancouver island, in their sight seeing.
It was from a stand of timber at Campbell river that a British Columbia_ fir was felled last summer, trimmed to a 105 foot flag pole and sent to Johannesburg, South Africa for the city's 50th birthday celebrations.
Attempts to transport the huge gift from the sea to Johannesburg by rail five hundred miles away, were abandoned in favour of roads because of the many sharp curves in railroad tracks. At some points only the tip and the butt of the pole rested on freight trucks.
A second problem arose with the erection of the pole, for nowhere in South Africa may the Union Jack take precedence over the flag of the Union of South Africa, and it is usual to erect twin flag poles.

There is, however, another matter which must be considered before the adoption of a national flag can follow. I refer to the meaning of the word "Canadian," and in this respect I should like to quote from "Canada 1937." Under the heading of racial origins, to be found at page 24, I find the following:
The object of securing information on racial origin at the census is to ascertain from what basic ethnic stocks the Canadian population, more particularly the recently immigrated population, is derived. The answer "Canadian" is not accepted under this heading, as the purpose of the question is to obtain, in so far as possible, a definition of "Canadian" in terms of racial derivation. It is clear that to accept the answer "Canadian" to the question on racial origin would confuse the data and defeat the purpose for which the question is asked.
May I suggest that the census taker could readily ascertain racial derivation by asking information as to the parentage of the individual, which I have no doubt would be supplied in all cases. As there is no provision on the census tables of Canada for the enumeration of Canadians, it is apparent that the paragraph just quoted from "Canada 1937 is a subterfuge, an explanation which does not explain but which accentuates the omission of the word "Canadian" from the official record. As we all know, were Canadians enumerated on the census, some provision would necessarily have to be made for Canadians to exercise their franchise at the polls as Canadians. Therefore I consider it somewhat of an anomaly that we should be discussing the adoption of a national and official flag for Canadians when even the hon. member for North Battleford is not officially a Canadian. Of course something is wrong and I suggest that we make it right. Is it true, as the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Kuhl) says, that there was no confederation or federal union? I leave the questiou with you:	Are we still a colony?

Mr. Speaker, I feel strongly about this question, but I shall endeavour to follow the excellent example of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) and couch my views in moderate and dispassionate terms. The resolution reads:
That in the opinion of this house, a special select committee be appointed for the purpose of considering the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag, representing Canada as a whole, thereby symbolizing the dominion as an equality partner in the commonwealth of British nations.
As was pointed out, it would be ridiculous to pretend that by adopting what is referred to as a distinctive Canadian flag we would be jeopardizing the position of the dominion in

A Canadian Flag
the empire or be weakening the part that the empire plays to-day in the affairs of the world. To say that would be putting the situation altogether too strongly. My objections to the resolution, which I shall state simply and shortly, are these: There never has been a time in the history of the world when the British Empire played such an important part as it is now playing in the preservation of such world peace as still remains and in the observance of fair play and justice and all that Christianity stands for. Therefore, this is the time when everything that we in this dominion can do to identify ourselves with the British Empire as closely as possible should be done.
One way in which we can foster and strengthen that bond is by exercising what I deem to be one of our greatest privileges, the flying wherever and whenever possible of the union jack. Unfortunately we are subjected to many influences which tend to weaken our imperial connections. The radio and the press of the country to the south are constantly disseminating influences that are in no sense of the word imperial, let alone Canadian. As an antidote to these often undesirable influences we have the union jack. To do other than fly it when and where we may, would in my opinion be bad policy. Something is said in the resolution about a distinctive Canadian flag. The union jack was sufficiently distinctive for the 60,000 men who laid down their lives for Canada in the great war. It is distinctive enough for me and, I believe, for the vast majority of those whom I represent.
There is another practical consideration. I do not think the mover of the resolution or any one else will deny that the most desirable type of immigrant we can get is the immigrant from the old land. Those are the immigrants whom we wish to attract above all others. Surely it would be a consideration in the minds of such people if they knew that when they reached our shores they would still find floating in the proudest position of all the emblem to which they had become accustomed. In some of the press references which the hon. member for North Battleford read into the record something was said about silly sentiment in discussing this question. Whenever we discuss a flag, whether it be a Canadian flag, the union jack or any other flag, a certain amount of sentiment must enter into our deliberations. There is a strong feeling of sentiment for the union jack. My hope is that it will be preserved and increased because it is an honourable sentiment.
There is sentiment in our feelings towards Shakespeare, Milton, Shelley and Burns, and
the works of these men arouse the same feelings deep in our breasts as are aroused when the union jack is mentioned. Therefore, for my part, Mr. Speaker, I deplore any move to fly any other flag than the union jack. In my opinion the motion is untimely, and such a motion would, in my view, be untimely at any time. I shall vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasant duty to compliment the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh),first, upon the appealing and convincing way in which he has presented his case to the house, and second, upon his tenacity in bringing up again and again in the house and promoting this most laudable project, which unfortunately so far has not met with the approval of this chamber. The perseverance and energy of the hon. member were not unknown to me because I saw him at work in his constituency of North Battleford, where I lived for many years, and where I am proud to say I had occasion to vote for him. As one who is no longer interested in his constituency I wish to tell the hon. member for North Battleford that not only in his constituency but in many other parts of Canada, probably -owing to his attitude in connection with a national flag, he is looked upon as a true, devoted and broad-minded Canadian.
I saw fit to make these few remarks with regard to the hon. member for North Battleford, because a decision such as the one we are about to take might seem queer, even wrong in the estimation of those who, though I believe they are in- good faith may consider it as a sacrilege, as it were, the fact of seeking to change in any way the British flag in order to have a strictly Canadian flag.
While I have the opportunity, I take great pleasure in paying my own and my constituents' compliments to the right hon. the Minister of Justice. I wish him health, happiness and success on this 34th anniversary of his coming to this house. These wishes are all the more sincere since the success of the Liberal party, the government and the country are so closely connected with the success, the happiness and the good health of the right hon. Minister of Justice. They may, to a certain extent, smack of selfishness, but I may assure the right hon. Minister of Justice that they are nevertheless profoundly sincere.
The reason I am taking the liberty of saying a few words in support of the motion introduced by the hon. member for North Battleford, is because I believe Canada has reached such a measure of self-government
A Canadian Flag

that we should enjoy all the essential characteristics which such autonomy entails. It may be-and I share this opinion-that we ought to retain substantially the character of the British flag, but we should make it distinctly Canadian by adding to it our emblem, as, for instance, the maple leaf. I wish to express my admiration for the British flag which, for many years, and even many centuries, has victoriously flown all over the world. We must admit that under the protection of that flag, except for the bad treatment that was meted to us in the early days of British domination, we enjoyed liberties and privileges of which we would certainly have been deprived under many another conqueror. The crosses of St. Andrew, St. George, and St. Patrick which are to be found on the British flag well indicate the union and cooperation which bind together the oldest members of the empire, and they also show that these elder members of the British Empire wished to have their emblem on the British flag. I think it is expedient that Canada add her own emblem so as to show that it is also her flag.
Since the other colonies, or I should rather say the other members of the British commonwealth have their own flag, why should not Canada have hers? As the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) said a moment ago. we must admit that in a discussion where feelings intervene, reason and logic do not always prevail. But since we are only seeking to add our emblem to the union jack, I think there is no ground to protest against adding to the old flag anything that would make it more attractive and more characteristic in the mind of Canadians. Besides, the lack of a distinctive Canadian flag is a paradox, an anomaly. A proof of this is the fact that, in those countries where Canada maintains legations, she must create some kind of a flag different from that of the empire through the addition of the Canadian coat of arms. Thus, Canada has a flag, outside its territory, but she has none for her own citizens.
On the other hand, the empire is not a federation. I do not think, either, that the idea of centralization has met with such a measure of approval among Canadians, that the latter should be willing to keep forever as their own the mother country's flag. A Canadian flag would no doubt hold much mere attraction for Canadian citizens. Such a flag would appeal much more to the imagination of children and better arouse their national pride. It would form a link that would unite more closely the French and English speaking native born Canadians with those who are simply naturalized Canadians. The thought or

ambition of those people who came to our country was not simply to become British subjects. I rather believe that they were determined to become plain Canadian citizens. Again, who could deny the fact that every nation must have her own flag. It is futile, if not ridiculous, to cast doubts upon anyone's loyalty in such debate. I reseut the suggestion that those who would adopt a Canadian flag have no attachment or loyalty towards the crown. This is not definitely stated but it is hinted, or insinuated, and every one can read between the lines; on the other hand, every one is quite free to say or think whatever he pleases. And I shall take the liberty, and avail myself of this opportunity to say that I am neither ashamed nor afraid to state that, while second to none in my loyalty towards the crown, if the interests of the mother country should ever happen to conflict with those of my native country, without the least hesitation, I would devote myself body and soul to Canada.
In reality, the opposition against the adoption of a Canadian flag is caused by imperialistic feelings. Let us hope for the day-'the sooner it comes, the better it will be for us all -when it may be possible, in our country, to discuss matters of interest solely from a Canadian viewpoint. Meanwhile I believe the best way of being a good British citizen is to remain a good Canadian.
There are in Canada groups whose traditions are not identical. It would be neither wise nor fair to wish for the disappearance of those traditions, but these different racial groups must meet upon a common ground. A national flag, along with our splendid national hymn, would provide this common ground and constitute a closer bond first between the provinces-they need it-and then between native born Canadians and naturalized Canadians, who should all be proud, at this stage of our history, to declare as a matter of principle that one country is enough for any man and that, from a practical viewpoint, the boundaries of their true fatherland should not extend beyond those of Canada.

I first will address myself to some of the remarks made by the mover of the resolution (Mr. McIntosh). If I understood him correctly he said that in 1933 a resolution similar to that which is now before the house was withdrawn because of the distress in the cities and the serious condition in the country. If that reason was effective in 1933 it is a first class reason for withdrawing the resolution to-day. I am sure that conditions in the constituency of the hon. member and other parts of the

A Canadian Flag
west are not so gratifying that this house can afford to waste its time debating an educational or academic motion of this kind. People in the west are crying to Ottawa for measures, whether they be the building of reservoirs, diverting rivers, or other constructive operations that will bring relief to the troubles caused by the drought; they are not, I believe, very much interested in the question of a flag, but are more concerned with their own pressing difficulties. I know very well that that is the situation in the east, and I am sorry to observe that while conditions did improve for a time, in the last month or two they have been getting worse.
Yesterday I spent the day with some friends in a railroad town not far from Ottawa and had a conversation with three railroad men. One of them remarked, "I see that the house is going to debate a resolution in connection with the flag. I want to tell you that so far as I am concerned, not only is the union jack good enough for me, but I am much more interested just now in getting a job." He said that fifty of the engine repairers in the town I am referring to had been laid off from the car shops because the large new locomotives are so powerful that they can run from Detroit to Toronto, and from Toronto to Montreal without a change. This man remarked to me, "As far as we are concerned we are interested in getting jobs at the present time; we are not interested in you men down there wasting your time debating a question which at best is only an educational question."
The hon. member who proposed the resolution quoted certain expressions but did not use them himself. I wish to compliment him on the mildness of his language and on the way he said what he had to say. Some of the quotations he used, however, intimated that anyone who has the nerve to oppose this resolution is prejudiced, that to do so is absurd and could have no other motive than a silly sentiment; he also produced a clipping which applied the word "ridiculous" to anyone presuming to oppose the motion. I do not intend to be deterred from what I have to say by any such expressions, neither do I believe such terms would be employed by the hon. member himself. On the other hand, respecting as I do the views of other hon. members, I expect them to respect mine.
I recall the hon. member said that the sentiment throughout Canada favouring the adoption of a so-called distinctive flag was almost unanimous. Before I sit down I shall
be able easily to show that that is not so; that on the contrary, opinion against the change is much stronger; that the organization which is responsible, as I see it, for creating the agitation to induce someone to bring this type of resolution before the house has for several years past been engaged in advocating a new flag, and that its late president, to whom I shall refer later, resigned because he believed that that organization was advocating the disruption of the British Empire. I do not argue that such a result would follow the adoption of a new flag-far from it. I am merely repeating what some of those in the organization behind this movement have been quoted as saying.
The hon. member who moved the resolution said that the Saskatchewan weekly papers are unanimously in favour of this proposal. With his powerful eloquence and his position as an outstanding editor in the province, if he went to a meeting of the Saskatchewan Weekly Newspapers Association and could not persuade them to adopt his resolution, or at any rate to support his point of view, I should be surprised.
I was not there.

Well, the weekly newspaper which the hon. member so ably edits lauded such a resolution. Am I not right in that? His views are well known in Saskatchewan. He has said something about Newfoundland. I must correct him in that particular, because on a trip to Newfoundland I discussed the flag situation with the commission. I found that the union jack is the flag used on land, and on the water they have a similar flag to ours, using their coat of arms on their blue ensign in much the same manner as we do, as well as on their red ensign.
We have already had two suggestions as to what could be put on a new flag. One was a maple leaf, which is a wonderful emblem. The beaver was also referred to, I believe by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Elliott) as a suitable emblem to place on the flag. But I should like to call attention to what was said by the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts), and I agree with it, that as it is we have sufficient difficulty in this country in trying to maintain a sentiment of loyalty to Canada, and a sentiment for the maintenance of Canada as part of the empire. There is no question that some are affected by the press of the republic to the south making jocular references to our traditions, our government and our king. We are also exposed to radio influences; I have myself heard many speeches delivered over the radio to which it was not very pleasant for a Canadian to listen.
A Canadian Flag

I endorse, therefore, what the hon. member for London has said, that in this matter we should go very slowly about doing anything that would tend to break down our sentiment towards the union jack and the old land.
As I have so far been for the most part replying to what has already been said in the debate, Mr. Speaker, if you will call it six o'clock I will give my own views when the house resumes after recess.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess

Mr. Speaker, just before the house rose I believe I said that :n view of the peaceful penetration of this country by newspapers from the republic to our south and by radio programs from the same source- and I might also add by commerce-in my judgment we should be very careful about starting anything new that might in any way weaken our adherence to our traditions and those of the empire to which we belong.
Perhaps it would be best right at the commencement of my remarks to correct a statement often made, which I think we have all read in the literature that has been sent to us recently by an organization which is pronouncedly against the union jack. I believe it fitting that at this moment I should point out that we have three official flags in this country. The one that was made official first is the blue ensign, which was made an official flag for Canada's government marine by the Colonial Defence Act of 1865. That flag bears on its fly the Canadian shield. The second official flag is the Canadian red ensign, which is used by our merchant marine on the seas and the lakes. That red ensign was ordered by an admiralty warrant in 1892. I might just interject here that when the house rose, someone, I have forgotten who, intimated to me that he felt that Canada ought to have a flag, and apparently he meant a distinctive flag, because if he went to Montreal or elsewhere and saw ships coming in, he could not tell from the flags which were Canadian ships. That is not correct; his information was wrong, and I desire to correct him. I now say that all Canadian merchant ships have flying at the stern the Canadian red ensign. Then, of course, we have the union jack, which in 1912 was ordered by the Secretary of State for the colonies as a land flag for Canada. So we have three official flags: the union jack on land, the red ensign with the Canadian
[Mr. MacNicol.)
coat of arms on the fly for our merchant marine, and the blue ensign with the Canadian coat of arms for our government marine.
I might say that when I was overseas last summer, in anticipation of the probable reintroduction of this resolution, which I believe has been before the house now on six or seven different occasions, I endeavoured to find out everything possible about the origin of those component parts which go to make up our flags and the heraldry associated with them.
I went back into antiquity as far as I could, visiting the signal offices of the Admiralty, the factories where they make the admiralty flags and the record offices of the great newspapers in London as well as the great magazines such as the Illustrated News, the Graphic and others. I wanted to try to disprove to my own satisfaction the statement that the union jack on land is not a distinctive Canadian flag; I wanted to disprove the statement that our red ensign with the coat of arms on the fly and the blue ensign with the coat of arms on the fly were not distinctive Canadian flags.
I have convinced myself, in any event, that they are more distinctive to Canada than almost anything of which I can conceive; that is, if one considers that a flag, to be distinctive of a country, must at least appertain to the races that go to make up that country. I will say this, that the more I searched and the further back I went into antiquity, it appeared to me that the race that had the most to complain about, as far as flags go, was the English race itself. The English people themselves would have more right to complain about their flag not being distinctly British, or ours not being distinctly Canadian, than any other race. Take, for instance, the union jack itself, with its three crosses. St. George's cross was originated not in England but in Asia Minor. The Greeks used it long before the English did. Of course they used a white cross on a blue field, while the British used a red cross on a white field. It is called St. George's cross because of the martyrdom, according to legend, of St. George on April 23, 361. St. George's cross on a flag was brought to England in 1194 by a Norman king, Richard I, on his return from the crusades. It was not of English origin at all; but the English, being broad-minded and steeped in business above everything else, were not perhaps so particular about the ordinary things, and were happy to obtain it. As I have said, that cross was introduced into England in 1194 by Richard I, a French-Nor.man king.
Then take St. Andrew's cross. That is not Scotch at all; but the Scotch, being receptive also, were willing to take perhaps almost any-

thing worih while. St. Andrew was martyred at Patros in Greece in 69, and according to legend about 370 the relics of St. Andrew were found on the W'est coast of Scotland.

I did not mean that the cross was adopted then. It was used in 740, I believe, by King Fergus, or some other king.
Then we have St. Patrick's cross. How much Irish is there about that? The Irish are also a fine race, and are willing to take anything that is good. St. Patrick himself was born in Scotland according to legend; but so far as the legend goes he went to Ireland and then to France. History says that his father was a magistrate for the Romans in the fourth century. Whether or not his father was Roman I do not know; but it is said that his mother was French, and St. Patrick's cross was introduced in Ireland about 1169 by the son of a Welsh king. In other words, the English themselves got their cross last. The Scotch got theirs in 740, the Irish in 1169 and the English in 1194.
As far as these crosses go, they are anything but English. Why there should be any feeling against the three crosses on the union jack is something I cannot comprehend. So far as the armorial bearings and the shields on our flags go, what is there about them that is English or Scotch or Irish? Again, the old country took advantage of something that was very good; they appropriated it, and finally used it on their flags. I believe it was stated in the circular sent out by the Native Sons of Canada that a flag bearing St. George's cross was the first English flag. No such thing! The early English did not have a flag. The Romans brought their flag to England, on which was a dragon or a lion. The Romans themselves had in turn acquired the symbol of a lion or dragon from Parthia, part of present Russia. In other words, the lions on our flags are not English. Originally they were brought in by the Romans from Parthia.
So it will be at once apparent that we have quite a mixture in our flags. Richard I, following the Norman procedure of having a lion on a flag, placed the Norman lion on the English armorial bearings. Then, how did we happen to get the fleur-de-lis on our flags? No hon. member will say that that is English. No; it is a very beautiful flower, and it is French. It was placed on the English arms by Edward III in honour of his French mother.
We see, therefore, that we have the fleur-de-lis from the French and the harp from
Ireland. I am convinced that the English are certainly a broad-minded and generous race. As I said before, if any race has a right to complain against its own flag, then it must be the English. But they are not complaining; they are just sawing wood, and going ahead. I had expected to see every French Canadian member in the house stand up and speak against the motion. I must say that I could not understand the two hon. members who have already spoken. If they understood that the flag is more French than English they would say, "That is our flag, above any other."
When William the Conqueror landed in 1066 he brought a flag with him. I was anxious to learn what kind of flag he had. Then I searched the records of antiquity to find out what kind of flag the Britons had. Hon. members will recall that, as history relates, it was the Saxon Harold who fought against William. On Harold's flag was found a dragon, copied from the Roman flag. He was supported at Hastings partly by men of Kent, on whose flag there was a white horse. The white horse had been the emblem of the Jutes and Westphalians.
May I point out that if any flag in the world is cosmopolitan, certainly it is the union jack. I say it should be accepted as our land flag, and as our water flag we should retain the red and blue ensign carrying our armorial bearings. Those flags should suit everybody, and all races within our borders.
When William landed in England he carried with him a flag given to him by His Holiness the Pope, a yellow cross on a white field. It has been said that we must have something distinctive. Well, of what should our flag be distinctive? I have listened to speeches over the radio about Canada having a distinctive flag. Of what will it be distinctive, if indeed it is not distinctive of the races which go to make up the people within the borders of the country it represents? About the only race to which it does not refer is the English. It is more French than English. As I pointed out earlier, part of the flag is Parthenian since the lions were Roman, that is Italian and were adopted by the Romans from Parthia. There we have the cosmopolitan flag which should please every Canadian, no matter of what nationality he may be.
There is no other flag like it. Let us see what the other nations have. What will happen if this matter is given to a committee? I cannot help thinking what happened as a result of the splendid speeches made in the South African house. Their resolution was
A Canadian Flag

sent to a committee, and I cannot help thinking what came back from it. Of course I can say that perhaps the Canadian House of Commons is more intelligent than any other, and might bring in a better report. Personally, however, I should be very sorry to see anything of this kind sent to a committee.
Let us see what the other countries have. Most flags consist of either horizontal or perpendicular bars. The majority of them have three bars, and they are of almost all colours of the rainbow. On the flag of Albania there are three bars: crimson, black and crimson. On the Argentine flag there are three horizontal bars: blue, white and blue. The flag of Austria has three horizontal bars: crimson, white and crimson. On the flag of Bolivia we find three horizontal bars: red, yellow and green. The flag of Bulgaria carries three bars: white, green and red. On the flag of Esthonia there are three bars: blue, black and white. The colours are assembled in different ways.
Other nations have the three horizontal bars with an emblem superimposed. Then we come to the natisns with flags having perpendicular bars, and as an instance I refer to the flag of France, with perpendicular bars: blue, white and red. I have found flags of five nations having three perpendicular bars. In addition to these there are the flags with perpendicular bars having emblems superimposed on the centre bar.
We now come to the other types of flags. In this connection we might refer to the flag of Turkey bearing a crescent and a star, and the Egyptian flag with three crescents and three stars. We must not forget Old Glory to the south of us, with its forty-eight stars and thirteen bars. We find throughout the world a combination of stars and bars or bars and bars, either horizontally or vertically arranged.
No other flag has anything near the same combination as has the union jack, or our own red and blue ensign. Traditions behind these flags go back to the remotest past.
I am wondering why it should be necessary to take up more time in the consideration of this motion, and I would suggest that the hon. member sponsoring it might very well withdraw his motion, and let us get on with the business of the house.
By whom has this agitation been brought about? We know it is only an agitation, because the vast majority of Canadians are not as keenly interested in the flag as they are in some other matters. They are much more interested in getting jobs. The people in the western provinces are more interested in the rehabilitation of their farms. If we were

asked to adopt some measures along those lines I am sure we would be more likely to have the support of the unemployed workers in the east and the drought stricken farmers in the west.
However, the motion is before us and we must debate it. The agitation comes principally from an organization known as the Native Sons of Canada. I am a native son of the fourth generation. Although not in a direct line, some of my ancestral family were at Ticonderoga and at Quebec, so I do not have to defend my Canadianism, when it. is compared with that of others who can trace back only one or two generations.
What do the Native Sons of Canada have to say? We find that they sent out a booklet described as A Catechism on Canadian Status, from which I shall quote only a few questions and answers. This is one question:
As Canada now has no national flag-
Notwithstanding the fact that I have proven we have three-
-should it, when adopted, contain the union jack as a part of its design?
The answer is:
No. It would be entirely improper unless placed in the design so as to indicate that it was so placed for sentimental reasons only.
The next question:
Has Canada officially adopted any flag?
And the answer:
She has adopted a flag for the use of the governor general, and one to fly on Canadian government buildings in foreign countries.
Before I forget I should like to correct the mover of the resolution in his reference to Canada House. I went to Canada House many times while I was in London and every time I visited that building I used to crane my neck to see whether a flag was flying. As a rule when people in London want to go to Canada House or to our legation in Paris they do not bother their heads to look to see if the union jack is flying; they simply find out where the building is located, call a taxi at their hotel and are dropped at the door. I am glad to say that Canada House had more union jacks flying during the coronation than any other government building in London that I noticed. There were usually four union jacks flying, and frequently one red ensign. South Africa house always had the South African flag flying, but I might say that I never saw it without a union jack as well. The same applies to the buildings of New Zealand and New South Wales. People are not interested in what flag is flying at Canada House or at the Canadian legation in Paris.

A Canadian Flag
All they are interested in is the business they have to do at these places. I quote again:
Is not the flag flown by the Canadian merchant marine a Canadian flag? No.
That is the answer of the Native Sons of Canada in the face of the fact that two of the official flags in Canada are the governor general's flag and the Canadian red ensign.
The next question reads:
Should either of the two flags mentioned be considered as a Canadian national flag? No. Canada has no national flag.
Well, Canada has a national flag; in fact, it has three of them. The next question reads:
Is it proper that the union jack should be flown over Canadian government buildings? No.
Well, it is proper and it is the law of the land. What does this organization propose as a flag for Canada? I suppose every hon. member has received a copy of this catechism. And on the last page of this circular containing the president's address we are practically told that any man who opposes the adoption of a new flag for Canada should be treated as a traitor. That is fine language to use as regards any member of parliament. The flag proposed by this organization consists of a purple background with a maple leaf and crown thereon. Wherein does such a flag tell of the sentiment of the French Canadians, of the Scotch Canadians, of the Irish Canadians or of the English Canadians? There is not much on it representing what I stand for or what I want on a flag.
The hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) said that he had had a hundred, or was it a thousand flags sent to him? I have had quite a number sent to me, but most of them landed in the wastepaper basket. I show one with the union jack up in the corner and a maple leaf in the centre. A past president of the Native Sons of Canada has this to say:
I would not be a party to anything which, to my mind, would make the union jack appear ridiculous, as it does to me, in the flag of South Africa.
They have a union jack on the flag for South Africa, but it occupies only one-eighty-first of the total area of the flag. I shall not take time to discuss some of the other flags suggested as most of them are just something. This is a report of a statement made by a past president of this organization, Doctor J. Cotton:
"I have refrained for some time from attending meetings and my resignation will be sent in shortly." declared Dr. Cotton. "The original constitution of the native sons was against separation from the British commonwealth and annexation to the United States," he declared, but he added, about a year and a half ago a
catechism was issued through a group in the organization. This literature, he asserted, "would cause any person who is sane to believe that the native sons were against a British connection."
I am not against British connections; I am for British connections. Earlier in the afternoon the hon. member for North Battleford said the vast majority of the people of Canada were for a new flag. The Sons of England is an important organization and some time ago I understand they sent a resolution to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). I should like to quote from the Sons of England Record, as follows:
The copy of the proposed Canadian national flag was duly received and considered, and I was instructed to advise you that the members of the supreme council of the Sons of England Benefit Society are strongly opposed to any change in our flag, feeling that the union jack is good enough for Canada and is a flag that we are proud to live under.
That was the letter from the supreme secretary of the Sons of England to the national secretary of the Native Sons at Toronto. The Canadian Legion in my riding passed a unanimous resolution instructing me to oppose this motion. I think some attention should be paid to this organization. I attended a meeting of the United Empire Loyalists at which a resolution was passed endorsing the union jack as the national flag of Canada. Instead of sentiment being for a change, in my judgment it is far stronger against a change.
South Africa has two flags. As an hon. member to my left said, they always have to erect two flagpoles there as the law of South Africa states that the union jack and the union flag shall fly side by side. The Australian flag is made up of a blue ensign with the southern cross. The New Zealand flag is similar, the southern cross being arranged differently. The flag of Brazil also contains the southern cross. I have no fault to find with what has been done in other parts of the empire, but I feel that we have a flag of which we should be proud.
India has a rather attractive flag and one to which I have no objection. It is made up of the union jack with the Star of India on it surmounted by a crown. If the different countries in the empire could decide upon a uniform flag, I would not oppose it particularly. But the way we are going now, with each country adopting a different flag, we are going to end up with a hodgepodge. I made an exhaustive search into the origins of the Indian flag, the Malta flag and the Jamaica
A Canadian Flag

flag. In each case the union jack has been used with the respective coats of arms superimposed.
I should like to close by relating an incident which occurred during my visit to London. Perhaps you, sir, and other hon. members will remember the great banquet which was held by the borough of Westminster. That was one of the most elaborate banquets I have ever attended. There were about 100 tables, with from eight to ten people at each. The government took care to see that there would be visitors from different parts of the empire at each table. A nobleman from Malay sat close to me and I engaged him in conversation. After a speech by one of the great statesmen of South Africa I turned to this gentleman and said, "We have a wonderful empire." He had told me that originally his family were Chinese but they had lived in Malay for ten generations. I tried to write down from memory a few days later just what his reply was, and I shall quote from my note:
Yes, we have a marvellous empire. I often ponder about these islands.
Then, as if pondering, he added these words:
If these islands, with their culture and the knowledge of the arts and sciences, with their love of right, their respect for colour and creed, with their integrity and their valour were to suddenly sink beneath the Atlantic, the nations of Europe in dismay and madness would destroy each other. With Britain's strong restraining hand gone, nation would fly at nation, the last remaining one would be impotent, a shambles. I shudder to contemplate the tragedy that would befall Asia, befall India, befall Malay, should the flag of this country sink to rise no morej
If such a catastrophe as that did happen, Mr. Speaker, it would not matter much what flag was chosen by parliament to fly over this country because whoever got to us most quickly, and was stronger than we were, would see to it that their flag flew over Canada.
I close with the thought with which I commenced when the house met at eight o'clock. In view of the peaceful penetration of this country by the United States, by means of the radio, the press, literature and commerce, we should be very, very careful to do nothing to weaken the traditions upon which this countiy has been built, traditions, as I have tried to point out, that are steeped in the glories of the French, who brought with them from Europe their language and their culture to help build up this nation; and I appeal to my French-Canadian compatriots not to hasten, not to jump and vote

for this resolution, because certainly now is not the time to present a resolution of this kind with the condition this country' is in at present. I appeal also to my hon. friend from North Battleford to withdraw his resolution and concentrate his splendid energies and outstanding ability on supporting measures in this house which will make for the rehabilitation of those fine provinces of the west, and which will at the same time assist in rehabilitating and giving employment to thousands who are now unemployed.

Mr. Speaker. I have only two or three thougius to contribute to this debate. I had anticipated that I would have something to answer when the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) had taken his seat, but I am persuaded that the research which he made in the old land during the past summer must have more or less convinced him that the speech he made in the house in 1934 was not entirely right, because it seemed to me as I listened to the hon. gentleman to-night that he did not wax as eloquent or was as fluent as he was over the flag situation three or four years ago.
One expression he used was that the vast majority of the people of this country are not interested in this question of a national flag. When this question first came before the House of Commons back in 1929 or 1930 I was somewhat of the same opinion, but I have changed my mind since then. I have come to the conclusion that the vast majority of the people of Canada are interested in this question and are anxious that this parliament should do something towards adopting a national flag for this new nation-Canada.
I had an opportunity this past summer of attending two meetings of people of racial origins other than those of people from the British Isles, and I noted that the flags of the countries to which they originally belonged held a predominating position. I was interested, too, in listening to the speeches that were made at those meetings in connection with the countries from which these people came, and in their statements as to why they came to Canada. They believed that they could better themselves here. They apparently believed that they were going to help build up a new nation on this north American continent; that they themselves were going to play a part in its building up, and I wondered on those occasions why people who came here with such ambitions should not have an opportunity of honouring a national flag in their new land as they honoured the flag of the old land from which

A Canadian Flag
they came. These people now constitute a majority of the people in this country, for according to the 1931 census, the people from the British Isles and their descendants constitute a minority, and I believe that from 1931 onwards that minority will be found to be much smaller than it was in 1931. These people came here and brought with them the best traditions of their race, their best thoughts and culture, and they are trying to assist every other nationality that there may be in this land in building up a new nation in Canada.
I have no doubt, after talking to a good many of these people and their descendants, Who came here from other lands, that- they are prouder of what took place at the imperial conferences of 1926 and 1932 than we who constitute the British stock. They realized they were in a country where they were going to share in building up a new citizenship and a new nation. They are trying to play their part, and we are not being asked to do very much when we are asked to give them an opportunity of honouring a flag that they can use in place of the flag of their old land. Many of these people came from strife-torn Europe. From their childhood they may have been taught to harbour resentment against some other European country. They may not look upon the union jack with just that reverence and honour with which those of British stock view it, but they know it is a British possession-
And they should honour it.

And they do. But they may not look upon it with the same honour and respect and reverence that we do. Let us give them an opportunity to develop the pride they have in their new land and in the citizenship they are building for themselves. That is one thought, Mr. Speaker.
The next one came after the coronation ceremonies in England last year. I was interested in reading the newspaper accounts of them, and proud of the part that Canada played, proud to know just how Canada was honoured at that great pageantry of empire. I want to read to the house a few lines penned by a man who used to sit in the press gallery of this house, who happened to be in London at the time, giving his impressions of the position that Canada occupied in British eyes, even though she was the senior member of the commonwealth of nations at that great ceremony. He says:
Most Britons resent Canada sponging on the old land for a flag. Moreover Canada's poverty of national pride (if the British people did not ignore it) would sensibly diminish what might be called the glorious pageantry of empire.
And again:
It was irritating to a Canadian in England during the coronation celebrations to see this bogus Canadian ensign everywhere; to see Canada's ministers of state riding in motor oars on which the Lancashire-made emblem was flown. No doubt, if Premier Mackenzie King and his colleagues had done the right thing they would have asked that these illegal ensigns be taken down and would have pointed out to the British government that Canada did not want a flag of its own but preferred to use the British banner. Such a request almost certainty would have been refused. The British still have a keen sense of national pride. They want their own place in the empire and they would find it impossible to understand why the senior dominion desired to confuse its identity with that of the parent member.
Who wrote that?

To use a British flag at the great spectacle of the gathering of the empire at the Aldershot tattoo would be to confuse the spectators. Nobody would know that the soldier carrying a second British flag represented Canada . . . Unless a spectator was so close that he could see the maple leaf on their badges, a British flag would mean that here was another regiment of home troops.
In Britain, of course, this is an utterly impossible situation. A Canadian flag, in Britain, is a necessity. If one doesn't exist, it has to be invented. And hence, it is, that the textile manufacturers of the north country have discharged the function of the parliament of Canada and have produced millions of bits of bunting which are sold and displayed as Canadian flags. Incidentally, all the other dominions-Australia, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa have spared Lancashire this trouble.
That was at the coronation, Mr. Speaker.
Whose statement is that?
That was written by Grant Dexter.
I thought so.
That damns it.
A native son, I suppose.
I hope so. I have no doubt he is. Is the hon. member saying that being a native son is something to be ashamed of?
Has the hon. member any objection to a native son?
Of that type-yes.

He writes as follows in connection with his journey to the continent and what he saw and heard there:
At Amiens, in the cloistered stillness of the chapel of the cathedral, the Canadian flag question took on a different aspect. Britons, Australians, New Zealanders, Newfoundlanders,
A Canadian Flag

South Africans and Canadians died in the great battle which was fought a few miles to the east of the city in those terrible days of 1918 when the last desperate onrush of German troops threatened to snatch victory from defeat. Southeast of the city, in the little village of Moreul, the name of Canada is written on the hearts of the villagers; they repeat the name Canada as they would the name of the patron saint. Just outside the village are the woods of Moreul which were held by the Canadian cavalry brigade. No country ever paid a higher price in the blood of its manhood for any bit of land than did Canada for these few acres of grass and trees. . . .
One of the leading citizens of the city happened to be in the cathedral when it was visited and volunteered to act as guide. The writer put to him a question which haunts the battlefields. " Do you regard it as a miracle that men from the ends of the earth-from Australia, Canada, the United States, New Zealand, South Africa and elsewhere came here and died in the defence of land that could not possibly have any importance to them?"
	The guide replied, "Yes, a thousand
times yes. These men were called of God in the defence of civilization and we were specially blessed that our lives and our homes were defended. Here in our cathedral we have tried to 6how our gratitude not only to God but to the men who died."
He led the way around the altar to where, on one side of the lady chapel were hung the flags of those countries whose soldiers had stood between Amiens and the invader. He went on to explain that there was no flag for Canada and the people of Amiens deeply regretted this was so. Canada, alone, was missing. But it was not their fault. They had tried to obtain the Canadian flag. They had taken the matter up with the government at Paris and had been told that there was no Canadian flag. It would not be right, he said, to hang a second British flag. He felt and his fellow townsmen felt that this would be unworthy of Canada and. in any case, would be meaningless-since one British flag was there already. If the writer could assure him that there had been any change in this situation, the city of Amiens would write to Paris immediately. Unfortunately no assurances could be given. It did not seem right that the Canadian boys, of all who fell in the battle of Amiens, should not be remembered in this ancient and holy place.
Reading that article by Grant Dexter, I came to the conclusion that if I had an opportunity of speaking on the flag question in the House of Commons at this session I would embrace that opportunity. For the three reasons I have given, I hope that the house will see its way clear to grant the prayer of the resolution and appoint a committee to consider a flag. I also have received many cuts of flags, some of which will provoke discussion to such, an extent that I believe any committee appointed from this house will be able to work out a flag which will truly represent the new nation of the north American continent-Canada.

As a life member of the Imperial Order of

the Daughters of the Empire, I feel that I would not be doing my duty if I did not say just a few words on this question.
We are talking of the flag, the union jack, and of foreigners who come to this country. When they came here they came under the protection of the union jack, knowing what the union jack stands for on land and sea in Australia, in New Zealand, in India, in Canada itself. Surely they did not come thinking they were going to live under the protection of a newly made flag. Let those of us who perhaps think the union jack does not mean so much, who may be forgetting what the union jack typifies, what it means, what it holds, reflect that we have the tricolour of France in the red, white and blue; white, for purity of purpose; blue, for tenacity; and red, for steadfastness in time of trouble; the cross of St. Andrew, for the Scots; the cross of St. Patrick, for the Irish; and the cross of St. George, for the English. I ask all hon. members to stop and think before they tamper with the union jack, which has meant so much for ages past.

I want to compliment sincerely and highly the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) upon the attitude and energy he has shown over a good many years in bringing this resolution forward for discussion on the floor of the House of Commons. At first, it is certain, it was a thankless task; but there is no doubt in my mind that the fine ideals he has propounded and the wonderful publicity they have received throughout the length and breadth of this country, through this discussion on the floor of the House of Commons, have brought about a condition of public opinion wherein I am convinced that a majority of the Canadian people would like to have a distinctive Canadian flag, which, from their viewpoint, would consolidate their bonds with the other parts of the British commonwealth.
(Translation). Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) my most sincere congratulations on this, the thirty-fourth anniversary of his parliamentary activities in this house. May he be spared for many more happy years to his own family, as well as to the large Canadian community, who look to him with such confidence in the federal field.
(Text). I wish to say a few words to the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) for whom I have the greatest respect. For the life of me I do not know why this afternoon he took occasion to cast reflection on the whole House of Commons. It has always been a revelation, to me at any rate, to see the parlia-

A Canadian Flag
mentary system we have in Canada, a system that has been inherited from the mother of parliaments, Great Britain; and one interesting aspect of that system is the provision for private members' day. Apart from the activities of the government, and altogether irrespective of the party in power, it is always possible for members of the House of Commons to bring forward any questions in which their constituents and the countiy are interested and submit them for the consideration of the house. Private members' day is, in my opinion, one of the best safety valves that any democracy could have.
I can assure the hon. member for Davenport that we have not been wasting time in the discussion we have had during the past two weeks in the debate on the address. The hon. member, I suggest, should be the last man to have the audacity to say that during those two weeks we have been wasting the time of the house in discussing the speech from the throne. Of course, it was a foregone conclusion, not only because of the government majority in the house, but also because of the excellence of the legislation forecast in the speech from the throne, that the address would be carried. I did not participate in the debate on the address, but I found it instructive and illuminating. Why? Because, in this wonderful national forum, I could hear the representatives from every part of this far-flung dominion, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, express the views of their electors. Surely the hon. member would not say that those were lost days. The motion could have been voted down in one or two days, but this is an open forum where members can bring forward and discuss any questions they are interested in. There are many other resolutions, besides this one with respect to a distinctive national flag, that will be brought forward on private members' days, and one is glad to think that private members will have an opportunity to present their motions. The provision is a very wise provision, because it gives leeway to private members to present to the nation at large through the House of Commons the views of their particular constituencies, and allows the movers to present their particular viewpoint.
The hon. gentleman said that Newfoundland had no flag. I wish to correct him; Newfoundland has a distinctive flag. There is a union jack on it, and I agree with the statement that there is not a member of this house who would like to see the union jack disappear entirely from the Canadian flag that we shall
have eventually. On the flag of Newfoundland is the escutcheon of that dominion, with the words Terra Nova and other Latin expressions. The hon. member for Davenport was not correctly informed when he said that Newfoundland had no flag.

I do not recall having
said that Newfoundland had not a flag of its own. I did say that the land flag of Newfoundland is the union jack; their merchant marine flag is a red ensign with a coat of arms on it, and the government marine flag is a blue flag with a coat of arms on it. -

Canada has attained national status; but it has been well said that, unlike Great Britain, our history does not go back into the many centuries of the past; and while the union jack evokes the loyalty of all Canadians it is not a distinctively Canadian flag. So far as I am personally concerned, the tricolour suggests only the flag of France, and if I had any say about the matter I would rather have the flag that was flown under the old royalty. But it does not satisfy us, because they are not and cannot be our flags, these two flags of France.
I do not deplore the fact, as some people seem to do, that our neighbour is the great republic to the south of us. Many hon. members take occasion every now and then to cast slurs on the United States, but in my opinion we need have no regrets at being so close to that country. I do not take a back seat to anyone when it comes to loyalty to British institutions and to the British flag. I have studied the history of Britain and I believe I speak for all French Canadians when I say that they are absolutely loyal to British institutions and their ideals. But at the same time we belong to the British Commonwealth of Nations and Great Britain is absolutely satisfied to recognize our complete status as a nation. In other words, we must realize that the more intensely Canadian we are, the more British we are likely to be.
We have only to read what Lord Darling said when he visited Canada the last time- that the strength of the British Empire lies in the strict independence of its component parts and in its apparent weakness. We are not bound to Great Britain by any bonds of iron and blood. It is one of the striking revelations of modem history that, whereas twenty-one years ago the other nations of the world could not understand how it was possible for the British Empire to hold together without armies of occupation, the common loyalty of the people throughout the empire to the same ideals has been evidenced time and again in recent years. It was not any bonds of iron
A Canadian Flag

and blood that held us to the mother country during the war but purely and simply our common sympathy and the love we have for those "tight little islands" across the sea and what they represent. I myself, as a representative of the minority in Canada, rejoice in our freedom in both creed and language. This is the true spirit that helped to build that wonderful empire; it is the spirit that should animate all parliaments within the empire. Great Britain would be the first to welcome on the part of the Canadian people a distinctive flag of their own.
In August, 1928, during the Olympic games in Holland the governors were surprised, when young Percy Williams covered Canada with glory, winning the 100 metre race, to discover that Canada had no distinctive flag. Surely that is an anomaly.
We hear a good deal that is derogatory of the United States, but it would do many "little" Canadians good to visit that country more. It would not take them long after crossing the border to appreciate how intensely national the people there are, whether they are of German or Polish or any other extraction. They are all Americans, no matter whether their ancestors came from Germany, Ireland, England, or anywhere else. Unhappily, we in Canada do not cultivate that spirit sufficiently. The question has been asked, Who brought the immigrants into the section of the country I come from? Well, it was the old parties, Liberals and Conservatives, that brought them in. We must all share the responsibility in this matter. We are trying to make good Canadians of them, and they will be good Canadians if we give them the opportunity. In my section we have people from all parts of Europe, and they are intensely nationalistic. They have the greatest respect for their own flags, and when they come here they are surprised to find that there is not a distinctive Canadian flag; they cannot understand it. On many occasions I have seen some of these people parading with their own national flags. I asked one man why they did this, and in reply he wanted to know what our Canadian flag was, and said how gladly and quickly he would make it his own.
The hon. member for Davenport says that the legionnaires are opposed to a Canadian flag. I can assure him that there are thousands of fine legionnaires in my riding, and . I know that the great majority of them are in favour of such a flag for the good reason that they are both Canadians and good Britishers.
I also have Sons of England in my constituency, and I have spoken of this problem

to them. I have asked their opinion in regard to a Canadian flag, and almost always they gave me the same answer, that it was absolutely possible and feasible to be good Britishers and still have a distinctive flag for Canada. I am making these statements at this time, Mr. Speaker, because I do not want any innuendoes against the reputation of the Sons of England or any other section of our Canadian population, as all sections are naturally open-minded and broad-minded.
I do not desire to deal further with this subject to-night, Mr. Speaker; but I should like to express the fervent wish that it might be found possible at this session to send this resolution to a special committee, where it might be discussed on its merits, even though no legislation in regard to the matter were introduced this year. Finally may I express the sincere hope that eventually Canada, one of the jewels and the senior member of the British Commonwealth of Nations, will have a distinctive flag which will be absolutely Canadian.
Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Peel); Mr. Speaker, I have only a few remarks to contribute to this enlightening and instructive discussion of a matter which has been brought up in parliament to-day for the first time since I came here in 1936. I want to congratulate the mover (Mr. McIntosh) of the resolution. His presentation of his arguments showed careful preparation and an undeniable conviction behind his sentiments. But, unfortunately, I must say that I was unable to agree entirely with the arguments advanced by the hon. gentleman. I want also to congratulate the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) on his contribution to this debate. I am sure most hon. gentlemen will feel much better after listening to the hon. member for Davenport describe exactly where the various parts composing our flag came from. I think he went back just about as far as any human being could go; I was afraid he would not stop until he had the pillars of King Solomon's temple embedded somewhere in the flag.
What I have to say in regard to this resolution is said entirely in a spirit of toleration and with all good will towards the various nationalities throughout our country who are not of the same racial extraction as myself. I make no apology, however, for belonging to a family which originally came from northern Ireland. At the same time I desire to make my remarks this evening in a spirit of great tolerance, because after all that is one of the things most essential in Canada as far as our national unity

A Canadian Flag
and national progress are concerned. During my remarks on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I made the statement-and I still stick to it-that in this country there is just a little too much talk about national unity and such things and perhaps not quite enough action and work towards that end. I am not so sure that a question so controversial as that raised by this resolution is a proper question to be brought up at this stage of our national development. I am not dogmatic in connection with this matter; I do not profess to have all the solutions for this problem which has been brought before the house, but I do say that we must exercise the greatest care and caution at this time because this is a critical stage in our national life. A controversial issue of this kind-and I think I make this statement in all fairness-which does not affect the very livelihood of the people, their food and shelter, is something which I do not think should be interjected into the proceedings of the house at this time. It is a matter which I think could very well be left over until another time without in any way dealing with the question on its merits, as to whether there should be a change or whether the same old flag should continue to fly over Canada.
I want to give credit to the nobility of impulse and the sincerity of purpose not only of the mover of the resolution and those who have supported it but also of those great bodies of public opinion which no doubt are urging that there should be a change in the flag of our country at this time. I have no intention of casting any aspersions upon those holding such ideas. They may be just as worthy as mine; but I submit, most respectfully, that we should not accept that argument at this time. We must deal with these questions with broad common sense and vision. I have no intention of wrapping myself in the union jack in discussing this matter, nor have I any intention of arousing any latent sentiments which might not do justice either to the resolution or to myself. There are, however, in Canada two very well defined, strong viewpoints held by perfectly sincere and honest people, which viewpoints are diametrically opposed in regard to this question of our flag. While those views are held so strongly, and since this controversy is of such a disputatious nature, I would submit most respectfully that it would be a move in the best interests of Canada if the resolution were withdrawn and not brought up for discussion at this time.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, there is another cogent reason why the resolution should not 51952-28
be sent on to a special committee. There are many, many questions facing the parliament of Canada to-day. There are many matters of transcendent importance to the people of our land, and I notice that in 1933 the mover of this resolution, the hon. member for North Battleford. had something to say with regard to the withdrawal of his resolution at that time, very similar to what I am going to suggest to-night. I shall not attempt to read all that the hon. member said at that time, but at page 1837 of Hansard of 1932-33 the hon. gentleman said:
... I am going to ask that the house postpone its consideration of this resolution. The fact that many Canadians are without food, clothing and shelter causes me to withhold this resolution until some future occasion when it may be discussed under more auspicious conditions, thus helping rather than perhaps hurting a cause so near and dear to all Canadians strong in their national and empire zeal and faith. When this time rolls around I hope parliament will come to a flag conclusion that will redound to the welfare of this country.
To-night I take a similar view as to the propriety of this discussion. I believe to-day, as at no other time in my brief existence, the people of Canada are looking with eager and very critical eyes, on every move that is made in this parliament, because of the economic stringency through which many have passed and through which hundreds of thousands are still passing. While these matters remain for our consideration and these problems await solution, shall we as a house make ourselves ridiculous by attempting to discuss something which is not putting first things first?
In the resolution the mover, in all fairness and sincerity of purpose, whether deliberately or otherwise has put the cart before the horse. I say the resolution is not fair to those who are urging a change in the flag at this time. I believe the present situation is comparable with one where a city salesman, well dressed and riding in a shiny car, stops at a farmer's gate and, in order to sell the farmer a certain book, enters into conversation with him. The name of the book is Farming, And How To Make It Pay. At this particular time the farmer is trying to get the last two loads of hay out of the field before the rain clouds open. Without any reflection upon the book or the salesman, it is evident that a most inopportune time was chosen to make the sale, and the salesman was not likely to receive a warm welcome.
A comparable situation exists with respect to the resolution before us. I would implore the hon. member for North Battleford not to bring the matter before a special committee, because I believe the time is inopportune.

[DOT]134
A Canadian Flag

Whatever may be the merits or demerits of the resolution-and there is scarcely a resolution in which good and bad could not be found-I believe this is not the proper time for discussion.
Although I do not intend to enter into detail, I should like to point out, by way of caution and warning, that it is going to take all the tolerance, all the care and all the patriotism at the command of the Canadian people or a committee of parliament to evolve a flag which would meet with such widespread approval as the flag we now have. I leave that as a word of caution, because after all we have to be most careful in making changes of this kind. When it is a matter of bettering the conditions of our people I am certainly in favour of change, but may I close by saying simply that we can work towards bettering those conditions under the old flag. Let us leave the old flag as it is, without changing to a new one at this time.
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops): Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh) upon the able manner in which he presented the resolution to the house. I wish I had the powers of oratory displayed by hon. members who have spoken. At least in some respects I agree with the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and if by refraining from speaking on the question it were possible to relieve the distress of the many thousands in Canada who need help, I would take my seat at once. However, that would not follow.
I noticed, as the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) said, that for the past two weeks we discussed an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, well knowing that the address would be adopted. Despite our knowledge of that fact, ten days of the time of the house were taken up in a discussion of the amendment.
It seems to me that Canada has assumed the responsibilities of a nation, and she has the right to make decisions regarding her participation in world affairs. That right is vested in Canada's parliament, without regard to the decisions of the mother country. I was born in Canada. My father and mother were born in Canada. My grandfathers and grandmothers, great grandfathers and great grandmothers all came from Ireland. I am proud not only of the fact that I was born in Canada but, too, of my Irish ancestry. The Irish have always contended that it was their right and privilege to fight within the empire. But when the empire is attacked from without, that is another matter entirely. I have no fear for the loyalty of Canadian people.

It would be quite impossible to decide upon a flag which would meet the approval of all the people. It is not so long ago that "O Canada" was not sung at the opening or closing of concerts. Eventually people found out that the singing of "O Canada" would not make them disloyal to the empire, but that on the contrary it was an indication that they were more loyal. Then we entered into a controversy as to what version of "O Canada" would be sung. Even to-day all people are not united on that point. Eventually we shall all sing one version, but in the meantime the empire will not be disrupted nor will Canada be charged with disloyalty.
I cannot see why Canadians could be considered less loyal or less British if they were to have a distinctive Canadian flag. Last summer we were visited by the South African Lawn Bowling Club, and the members who came to Canada were amazed to find out that we have not a flag. Many designs have been suggested, and of course I have personal preferences. I should like to see the union jack and the maple leaf embodied in the new Canadian flag.
However I am more interested in the principle. The principle involved is that Canada should have a distinctive Canadian flag, and I think that this session of parliament should not dissolve without recognizing that principle. For these reasons I have much pleasure in supporting the resolution.
