speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, mention has been made during this debate of the fact that the resolution we are now considering has been brought forward in previous sessions, and that much of what has been said has been a repetition of previous discussions. In my opinion that is all to the good and, in view of the subject under consideration, most fortunate.
Wherever there is a suggestion of change or a suggestion of departure from custom, numbers of people find such a course unpleasant even to contemplate. It is only by degrees that many of us find it possible to free ourselves from that to which we have grown accustomed. The arguments which have been urged against having a distinctive Canadian flag have to a great extent been arguments associated with profound sentiment and tradition. While these considerations are admirable in themselves, they are not necessarily decisive. Especially in times of change, we must look not only to the past but also to the future.
II consider it fortunate, that the resolution has come before the house as a private member's motion. As has been said by one hon.

A Canadian Flag
I member, when the subject is presented in this { wnv hon. members generally have a sense of greater freedom of discussion. It removes the possible feeling of restraint which a government measure might occasion and permits much more in the way of a free and frank expression of view than -would otherwise be the case.	I agree with the hon. member for
Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) when he says that, -this debate has been characterized by an^ expression of views which will be distinctly helpful in the forming of public opinion on this all important question.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for North Batt.leford (Mr. McIntosh) for having brought forward his resolution thus early in the session, and particularly upon the admirable manner in which he has presented the arguments pro and con. I shall not attempt in any way to review the discussions which took place on similar resolutions in previous years as those debates have been admirably covered by the hon. member for North Battle-ford. I would like, however, to call attention to the wording of the resolution. I was surprised to hear some hon. members express the opinion that the adoption of this resolution meant an immediate decision upon a design for a distinctive national flag. The question of design is entirely apart from anything that appears in the resolution. The resolution simply calls for a declaration as to the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag. If a committee is appointed and reports favourably upon the adoption of a distinctive national flag, and the committee's report is adopted, the question of design would then come up at a later time. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, a special select committee be appointed for the purpose of considering the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag, representing Canada as a whole, thereby symbolizing the dominion as an equality partner in the commonwealth of British nations.
The important words are "the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag." I cannot see why any hon. member of the house should be at all fearful about leaving to a committee of this house the consideration of the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag. The committee would be called upon to consider the expediency of making a declaration of that kind at this particular time. Undoubtedly it would take into account the fact that there may be considerable difficulty in getting agreement as to what design should ultimately be adopted for a distinctive Canadian flag. The possibility of such disagreement might conceivably be regarded as being so important that it might seem to the committee inadvisable to recOm-
-51952-28J
mend the adoption of a distinctive Canadian flag. Personally I do not think that such would be the case. All that the house is being asked to do at the present time is to permit a committee of its members to view the situation from as many angles as possible and to report back as to whether or not they feel the time has come when Canada should adopt a distinctive national flag.
The historic facts in reference to Canada's flag are really most pertinent in a consideration of this matter. They afford strong reasons, it seems to me, why we should feel that the time has come when Canada should have a distinctive national flag. There are also practical reasons of necessity which make this desirable.
Let me briefly outline a few of the facts. I shall seek to set them forth in as concise language as I can. Following the conquest, British immigrants to Canada brought with them the British flag and it was everywhere recognized as the emblem of the colonies as of the mother country. After 1801, the union flag, more commonly known as the union jack, became the flag of the empire. This situation remained unaltered until after confederation.
Some hon. members on the other side of the house have been speaking as though the union jack had always been the flag of Britain. A great deal of what they'themselves quoted went to show that only in comparatively recent times has the union jack been the flag of Britain. Only in 1801 did the union flag, commonly known as the union jack, become the flag of different parts of the empire.
After the formation of the Dominion of Canada the desirability of having a distinctive flag for use on Canadian government vessels became apparent and by order in council of February 28. 1870, the blue ensign, defaced by the Canadian coat of arms, was adopted for this purpose. This was confirmed in the King's Regulations and Admiralty Instructions, Article 123. In other words, a distinctive Canadian flag was found to be necessary with regard to government vessels and an order was passed as many years ago as 1870 to require that the blue ensign, defaced by the Canadian coat of arms, should be adopted for this purpose.
As long ago as 1870 we came to have a third flag, a recognition also of the necessity of having a distinctive flag. There were government vessels, but there wras also a merchant marine. With the expansion of the merchant marine the lack of a Canadian flag caused frequent difficulties and after some discussion
A Canadian Flag

the Lord's Commissioners of the Admiralty, were prevailed upon to issue a warrant, dated February 2, 1892, authorizing vessels registered in Canada "to wear the red ensign of Her Majesty's fleet with the Canadian coat of arms on the fly thereof."
This practice was confirmed in 1934 in the Canada Shipping Act, 24-25 George V, 1934, chapter 44, section 89. For some years after 1892, this flag was also in practice used on land as the Canadian flag and is indeed still employed in that way by many private citizens. After protests had been made, its use on government buildings in Ottawa was discontinued in 1904 and the union jack was hoisted in its place. Until 1904 we were flying the red ensign on most of the public buildings of Canada.

That is right. In that year the practice was adopted of flying the union jack.
How was it that the union jack came to be called the official flag of Canada? It is interesting to note that apparently the union jack was never declared officially to be the flag of Canada until 1911. On April 12 of that year Colonial Secretary Harcourt addressed an official dispatch to the Governor General of Canada declaring that the union jack should be flown on land as the Canadian flag.

speechtext:
That is the
reason it is on this building. In the days when that office was still in existence, the colonial secretary indicated to the governor general of this country the flag that was to be used. But the office of colonial secretary has ceased to exist in so far as it is applicable to Canada. There remains of course a colonial secretary, but he no longer has to do with the affairs of the self-governing parts of the empire. For this purpose a new office has been created, that of secretary of state for the dominions. I would respectfully point out that there is a vast significance in this change of office, a significance which has its application to the question under discussion at the moment. The question is whether or not Canada, as a self-governing dominion with equality of status with Great Britain and the other self-governing dominions, should not have, as they have, a distinctive flag, instead

of having a flag which is the flag of the colonies of Great Britain and of none of the dominions save our own.
In 1911, under a memorandum of agreement between the British Admiralty and the Canadian government, ships of the Royal Canadian Navy were instructed and authorized to fly tne white ensign at the stern and the blue ensign, with the coat of arms of Canada on the fly, at the jack staff. This was confirmed by Canadian government order in council of December 16, 1911.
Difficulties having arisen in Canadian government offices abroad, due to the lack of a distinctive Canadian flag, an order in council dated January 26, 1924, was passed, authorizing the flying of the red ensign, with the Canadian coat of arms on the fly, "from all buildings owned or occupied by the Canadian government and situated without Canada."
So we have to-day the curious anomaly that the flag, which we fly in Canada as the official flag, is flying by virtue of some direction which came from the colonial secretary in Great Britain, whereas the flag, which Canada flies as her own flag on buildings outside Canada, is a different flag and is flown by virtue of an order in council which was passed by the government of Canada itself. If there were no other reason, I think that fact of itself makes it apparent that the time has come when a distinctive national flag, if one can be agreed upon, is in every way desirable so far as Canada is concerned.
Now what about the emblem itself that appears on the flag? The Canadian coat of arms used on the various flags consisted until March 31, 1924, of a shield upon which were quartered the arms of Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. On that date, as late as 1924, the new Canadian coat of arms which had been assigned to the dominion by royal proclamation on November 21, 1921. was authorized for use on the flags. Thus, the Canadian flag itself, so-called, when it is officially used in this way, is one that has undergone considerable change in recent years.
Hon. members who were in this house some sessions ago may recall that in 1925 the government announced the appointment of a committee of civil servants to consider the question of a distinctive Canadian flag. That committee had been set up by one of the government departments, the Department of National Defence. The fact that such a committee was set up at all may serve to illustrate one of the practical needs of a distinctive national flag so far as Canada is concerned. I have drawn attention to the fact that the British Admiralty found the necessity of having a distinctive Canadian flag so far as

A Canadian Flag
Canada's merchant marine was concerned. As flying developed in this country, the members of the air forces felt that it was desirable, in connection with the manoeuvres in which they would have to engage, that there should be some distinctive Canadian flag associated with their service. As hon. members know, there are, on occasions, manoeuvres when the forces are interchangeable as between different parts of the empire, for purposes of training, exhibition and the like. To distinguish the forces of one part of the empire from those of another in these manoeuvres it became obviously desirable that there should be a distinctive flag.
It so happened that the departmental committee which I mentioned a moment ago had a complexion which was not wholly congenial to all parts of the house and the country. It was a mere accident that it so happened that all of its members were found to be of one religious persuasion. Immediately a section of the press of our country interpreted that circumstance as evidence in itself of some evil design. It was therefore thought advisable that the committee should be discontinued, as it was shortly after its formation. But the purpose of the committee was a thoroughly practical, a thoroughly good and a thoroughly necessary one, namely, to see if it were not possible to work out some distinctive flag that could help meet the needs of the forces of the Canadian Department of National Defence. The fact that some years ago it was thought desirable, from the point of view I have indicated, to have the question of a distinctive Canadian flag considered by a committee of civil servants, seems to me to make it desirable that parliament should not delay longer in seriously considering the question, and at least taking the first necessary step to ascertain whether agreement can be reached as to the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag. I believe the fact that the committee made the venture it did, in the circumstances it did, has operated to postpone further consideration of the question in a way which otherwise would not have taken place. The suggestion that a committee of this house should consider the matter ought to make it possible for us to ensure the personnel of the committee being as representative as possible of all shades of opinion in this house. Such a course will enable the first step to be taken, certainly without any danger, and with a great deal to commend it.
There are many positive disadvantages and difficulties existent to-day in not having a distinctive Canadian flag. Certain of these
have been mentioned in the course of the debate to-day. Perhaps I may briefly summarize the outstanding ones.
First of all there is the necessity of a Canadian flag for use on Canadian official buildings abroad. I ask hon. members, if Canada is to have legations, and I assume that we shall expand our legations rather than contract them, if we are to have commercial offices in different parts of the world, is it not also desirable for us to have a distinctive flag of our own to fly over them? As it is. we have for the purpose only a make-shift flag to-day. We are not using abroad our national flag, the flag that is the national flag at home, the union jack. At the present time the Canadian marine flag is flown over official Canadian premises abroad.
We are thus faced with the anomalous situation of the Canadian government using one flag in foreign countries and another flag at home. This is an absurdity to be found in the practice of no other country.
On the other hand, would any hon. member suggest that we should have flying from the Canadian legation in Washington, for example, the same flag that flies from the British embassy in Washington? Take the position in Tokyo. Are we to have the same flag flying from our legation there as flies from the British embassy? The same thing applies in Paris. London itself makes the need even more self-evident. Are we to have flying from the Canadian building in London, in the heart of the city, simply the union jack, while across Trafalgar Square you see the flag of South Africa, and a little further along Northumberland street the distinctive flags of Australia and New Zealand? And where there are other government offices representative of other parts of the empire, you see their distinctive flags flying from their buildings. The very fact that we are confronted now with that situation seems to me to make it imperative that we should not longer delay consideration of the advisability of having a distinctive Canadian flag.
Mention has been made of our war memorials in France, in Belgium, in Great Birtain and elsewhere. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) read this evening some dispatches which bear out notes I had made to the effect that correspondents have frequently pointed out that in cathedrals in Europe, where the flags of the allied powers have been enshrined in memory of the men who fell in the Great war, no Canadian flag is to be found, although the name of Canada is included in the inscription which
A Canadian Flag

accompanies the flags. So long as the union jack is the only official Canadian flag available for such use, the dominion will continue to be unrepresented, because the union jack will already have been used to represent the United Kingdom.
Then there is the matter of the necessity of a distinctive flag for use at international conferences. At all such meetings, when the United Kingdom is represented, the union jack will be used by the delegates from London. Even when the United Kingdom is not represented, the union jack is indelibly associated with that country in the minds of foreign observers, and its use will not gain for Canada the distinctive recognition which a national flag is supposed to evoke. When both London and Ottawa are represented at such international gatherings, the use of the union jack by the Canadian delegates will tend to identify them as part of the United Kingdom delegation. Such use might well be resented by the representatives of the United Kingdom. We had this extraordinary anomaly at the time of the coronation and of the recent imperial conference, that when my colleagues and myself arrived in London we were met at the station by representatives of the British government who told us that they had placed automobiles at our disposal for the time of the coronation and the conference, as was done in Ottawa by the government of the day for the delegates who came here on the occasion of the conference of
1932.	Over the radiator of each of these automobiles was a Canadian red ensign. We were told that that flag had been put there so as to distinguish our cars from those of the other self-governing dominions and from the cars used by members of the British government. All the time we were in London we were, by the act of the British government itself, expected, wherever we went, if we were travelling by motor to travel in a car which carried, not the flag which on the authority of the British government is the flag of Canada within the dominion, but the flag which is flown outside the dominion and flown, not as is the case with the union jack in Canada itself, but under an order in council of our own government making a different provision. That of itself, as I have already remarked, is a most curious anomaly. It shows the necessity-the necessity from the point of view of the British government as well as our own-of Canada having a distinctive flag. I cannot see wherein there is any sacrifice of sentiment or loyalty in the desire on the part of its citizens that one's country should be known in other parts of the empire or in other countries of the world.
(Mr. Mackenzie King.)
There may have been a time when we were a colony, under the old colonial status, when we would perhaps have wished to use a flag that was symbolical, not only of the mother country, but of all the colonies as well. Having, however, reached the status of full nationhood, it becomes essential, if we are to be distinguished from other nations of the commonwealth, not to mention colonial possessions, that we have a distinctive flag of our own.
Reference has also been made this evening to the need for a distinctive flag at international athletic meets. At the Olympic games and the empire games, Canada in practice is now represented by the marine flag and not by the national flag. There is nothing to justify such abnormal practice except necessity. No other dominion and no other country would think of being so represented. At the Antwerp Olympic games in 1928 the confusion over the Canadian flag caused a great deal of trouble and no little annoyance.
I have already referred to the need of a distinctive flag by the Canadian defence services at home and abroad. When details of the Canadian military forces appear at home or abroad they carry the union jack as their national flag. This means that by many they are identified with or mistaken for imperial British forces, unless the observer is close enough to see the maple leaves on the uniforms, whereas the defence services of other dominions are all readily recognizable where they appear, as at the recent coronation services and other great occasions.
The red ensign with the Canadian coat of arms is used at sea. Surely it is absurd to argue that a distinctive flag for use on land is a sign of disloyalty when a distinctive flag is already in use on the sea.
I would conclude this part of what I have to say with the observation that the continued use of the union jack gives a false impression abroad, and particularly in the country immediately adjoining. The use of the union jack on anything that is distinctively Canadian in the United States does not help to emphasize the individuality of this country or its distinct nationality; it helps to submerge them altogether.
I do submit that, viewing the matter historically, viewing the matter sentimentally, or in any other way, the argument all lies in favour of recognizing that the time has come when we should very seriously consider the adoption of a Canadian national flag. I would point out that as our constitutional development has undergone considerable change, it is only appropriate that there should be in connection with that statutory change the change

A Canadian Flag
in other particulars which may be necessary to make distinctive in the eyes of the world the different dominions which now have the equality of status of which we speak so frequently.
There is no doubt that the great war more than anything else was responsible for developing a strong national sentiment. I believe that those who served overseas for the most part came back more zealous than any other proportionate element in our country to have a distinctive flag which would designate their own forces and help to let Canada stand henceforth in the place in w'hich she has the right to stand.
Coming to developments which followed the great war, developments on constitutional lines, we had first, as the most prominent of the declarations, relative to our position as a nation, the report of the imperial conference of 1926, which made quite clear the position which Canada along with the other dominions had attained. This report has been referred to frequently in previous sessions of other parliaments, but there are in the present house many hon. members who were not here in the last parliament, and it might be of interest to them, in this particular connection to hear words that appear in the prefatory part of this report of the interimperial relations committee, which was a committee of the imperial conference of 1926. Perhaps I should preface the reading of what I wish to quote, by saying that the chairman of that committee was the late Lord Balfour, as great an imperialist, possibly, as the British Empire had, but a great political philosopher as well, and one who was capable not only of viewing the past but also of glimpsing something of the developments of the future. The wording of this report seems to me to disclose the wisdom of this country speedily making a decision with respect to a flag which will be distinctive in its nature. The report reads:
The committee are of opinion that nothing would be gained by attempting to lay down a constitution for the British Empire. Its widely scattered parts have very different characteristics, very different histories, and are at very different stages of evolution; . . .
That is a point to which I wish to call attention particularly. The colonies are still at the colonial stage, they are still using the union jack which is the flag of the mother country; but the self-governing dominions, with the single exception of Canada, have all distinctive flags of their own. The report goes on, referring to the empire:
-while, considered as a whole, it defies classification and bears no real resemblance to any other political organization which now exists or has ever yet been tried.
There is, however, one most important element in it which, from a strictly constitutional point of view, has now, as regards all vital matters, reached its full development-we refer to the group of self-governing communities composed of Great Britain and the dominions. Their position and mutual relation may be readily defined. They are autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status, in no way subordinate one to another in any aspect of their domestic or external affairs, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown, and freely associated as members of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
A foreigner endeavouring to understand the true character of the British Empire by the aid of this formula alone would be tempted to think that it was devised rather to make mutual interference impossible than to make mutual cooperation easy.
Such a criticism, however, completely ignores the historic situation. The rapid evolution of the overseas dominions during the last fifty years has involved many complicated adjustments of old political machinery to changing conditions. The tendency towards equality of status was both right and inevitable. Geographical and other conditions made this impossible of attainment by the way of federation. The only alternative was by the way of autonomy; and along this road it has been steadily sought. Every self-governing member of the empire is now the master of its destiny.
I submit that, if these words had been used by a Canadian member of parliament a few years before this particular document was written, whoever had used this language would by not a few have been written down immediately as a separatist, as disloyal to the empire, and as wishing to make Canada a country apart from it altogether. The thought that we were masters of our own destiny seemed to be abhorrent to the minds of many of our people, who contended that the destiny of Canada could and should be determined only by what might be agreed upon overseas. That day fortunately has long since passed. Canada has come to feel that it is a national entity and that it is entitled to have its national individuality and characteristics known and respected and honoured as they should be in the eyes of the other nations of the empire and of the other countries of the world.
In considering the development which has taken place in the status of this dominion, we are not only justified at this time but are obligated to think very seriously of every aspect of nationhood and of what is essential to the assertion of it. Far from being a cause for separation, or a thought of separation, we should feel, and I believe we do strongly feel, that our national freedom, the free expression of our national characteristics and aims and purposes, is of all ties the one that holds us
A Canadian Flag

the most closely within that circle of communities which form the British Commonwealth of Nations.
What is embodied in this resolution of the imperial conference of 1926 later found expression in the Statute of Westminster. The Statute of Westminster sets forth very definitely certain alterations made in order to remove anachronisms which in one way or another were unsuited to the new relationship of empire as they have developed. There is a more recent development, which lends a new emphasis to the subject we are discussing to-day. I refer to the wording of the oath administered at the coronation of King George VI and sworn to by his majesty himself. On that occasion, for the first time, His Majesty the King undertook, with respect to the relations of the crown to the dominions, to govern each of them according to its own laws and customs, and the coronation oath specifically enumerates the different dominions. I made a reference to this when speaking on the address. May I read to the house anew the oath which was administered to His Majesty King George VT, the obligations of which he promised solemnly to fulfil:
Will you solemnly promise and swear to govern the peoples of Great Britain, Ireland, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the Union of South Africa, of your possessions and the other territories to any of them belonging or pertaining, and of your Empire of India, according to their respective laws and customs?
Thus His Majesty the King declared that he would govern Canada according to her particular laws and customs, exactly in the same manner as he would govern Great Britain according to her own laws and customs. Why should not custom of all self-governing dominions be the flying of a distinctive flag that helps to identify one from the other?
Please note that all of the other self-governing dominions already have their distinctive flags. We are not now debating the question whether or not there should be one flag for the whole empire. That question has already been settled by the facts of the case. I believe it was the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNieol) who said that he would like to see one flag for the whole empire. Perhaps a good many would. But that is not the point at issue; it does not come up at this time and is not likely to come up for the reason that already Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, the Irish Free State and India has each a distinctive flag of its own. The Dominion of Canada is the one exception. The point we have to consider is whether or not we should longer remain the one exception, the one self-governing part of

the whole British Empire that has not thought it advisable to adopt a national flag. That is the question, and it seems to me that in the light of the past and having regard to the future the question admits of only one answer, which is that the time has come when we should adopt a distinctive national flag.
The perspective of years makes it essential that we should consider at this time the very important question that is now before us, Canada is a growing country. She is going to increase in world influence as well as in numbers and in wealth. She will need more and more her own national emblpm.. Moreover, we can consider this question now more opportunely, I believe, than at any other time. I suggest that it is important always to bear in mind that there are times and seasons for all things. There have been times in the past when to bring forward a resolution such as the one now before us would have been to create misunderstanding as to motive, a misunderstanding in other parts of the world as to the significance of the motion itself. I might go so far as to say that had Canada been the first to take such a step, her action might have been misunderstood in other parts of the empire and of the world. If Australia had not already adopted a national flag; if New Zealand had not already adopted one; if South Africa and the south of Ireland had not already adopted their own distinctive flags, then there might be some reason for hon. members to say, "Let us be careful lest we set a precedent which will be followed in other parts of the empire and lead perchance to the dismemberment of the British Commonwealth of Nations." But the fact is that as a result in part of each having its own distinctive flag the other members of the . commonwealth have come to have a new pride, not only in their respective countries but in that free association which they together enjoy in the British Empire. In these circumstances, the question for us to decide is whether so far as this matter is concerned we shall remain in our present state of isolation, or, like them, adopt for ourselves a flag which shall be the emblem of our distinct personality as a people.
Let me conclude with these words. There has never been a time, I believe, when the relations between Canada and the mother country were so cordial, so completely friendly, helpful and cooperative in every way as they are at the present time. The present is the time, then, to consider this question. It will not be disposed of, in my opinion, until it is settled in Canada as it has been in the other dominions. If we do not settle it now, some issue may arise in the

A Canadian Flag
course of a few years which will provoke another discussion and lead to the settlement of the question in a manner that may be misunderstood elsewhere. To-day there is no possible danger of misunderstanding on the part of anyone in this country, in Britain, in Europe or elsewhere in the world, as to what Canada has in mind in seeking to have a distinctive national flag.
So, Mr. Speaker, I feel we are greatly indebted to the hon. member for North Battle-ford who has brought forward this resolution at this time. I hope the hon. members who have expressed quite sincerely their views in opposition to it will feel, once they understand that the motion does not go as far as they thought it did, namely the length of deciding at this time on the design of a national flag but only asks that a committee be appointed to consider whether the time is not opportune for adopting a distinctive flag, that they may support the resolution and allow it to be unanimously adopted.

Mr. Speaker,
I have no intention of addressing the house on this question. I think the matter has been quite fully covered, but in case the resolution should be adopted I should like to offer a suggestion to the mover. I am not declaring my stand on the resolution itself; that is not necessary until the time comes, but I should like to know if the mover would be willing to add the words "with the union jack prominently included in the adopted-design," so that the resolution would read:
-adopting a distinctive Canadian flag with the union jack prominently included in the adopted design-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The committee might include that if it wished.
Then it would be obligatory on the committee to include the union jack in that design. If that could be done I think it would be a sound step, and I make the suggestion in the interests of safety.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
of considering the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag-
With all deference to my hon. friends who take a different view, I cannot see that the house should not set up a committee to consider the advisability of anything. I see
A Canadian Flag

no reason why it should not. Just why the House of Commons should not name a committee to consider the advisability of adopting a distinctive flag by the Canadian people I cannot see. I confess that I may be very wrong in the view I take, but surely the house can safely ask a committee to consider the advisability of a distinctive flag. It will be observed that the resolution does not go further than that; it states:
-for the purpose of considering the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag, representing Canada as a whole, thereby symbolizing the dominion as an equality partner in the British commonwealth of nations.
The last part is surplusage, as far as the resolution is concerned; I think that would be agreed at once. All that we are asked to do is to name a committee to consider the advisability of this action being taken, not to determine what the action shall be. I was surprised that the hon. member should have put forward his resolution in those terms, for Mr. Dickie's resolution was far, far wider than that. As will be remembered, Mr. Dickie's resolution provided for the flag itself. I referred to it a moment ago, and I might take time to read it again in order that there may be no misunderstanding. Mr. Dickie's resolution was as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, a national flag representing the Dominion of Canada should be adopted; and that in any design for a Canadian flag the union jack must he conspicuous.
That resolution did two things. First it said, "We must pass a resolution for the adoption of a Canadian flag," and, second, it said that in that flag the union jack should occupy a conspicuous place. That language was used, with respect to the latter part of that quotation, by the present Prime Minister himself, as well as by the hon. member for North Battleford. In view of what has been said I can see no reason why in the interests of harmony it might not be well for the hon. gentleman, with the consent of the house, to add those words to his resolution. Offences must need come, but woe unto him through whom they cometh. If by adopting the suggestion which has been made any difficulties would be overcome, I think it might be well that the suggestion should be acted upon.
Upon the large question, I expressed an opinion in the house some years ago that I believed it was desirable, as I do to-night, that the country should have some flag by which it could distinguish itself from other parts of the world. But that question is not one which should be debated in the house.
The resolution does not deal with that. It asks that a committee-not this chamber- consider the advisability. When the coin-
mittee has made its report it will then be for the chamber to consider whether or not that report will be adopted. The history of the flag, its use on sea and land, have been considered here to-night. But I would like to say to the Prime Minister that if he will look into the matter he will find that a colonial secretary did not send a dispatch to the parliament of Canada, without correspondence having taken place. Sir Wilfrid Laurier at that time was contemplating going to the imperial conference, and one of the problems which confronted them had to do with our naval force.
The question was plainly put as to what flag should fly, for instance, on our parliamentary buildings, when we were in session. Although my memory is not sufficiently clear on the point at this time, I know it was not a bolt from the blue on the part of the colonial secretary as to what the flag should be. Colonial Secretary Harcourt did not do business in that way. What was done was in response to an inquiry, just as in the case of the +able of precedence, and other questions, when requests are made of the colonial office. The colonial secretary transmitted his views to the governor general.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But it was the colonial secretary.

Of course. Nobody else could do it at that time. They ask the king; the king refers it to his government, and the colonial secretary is of course the person who makes the reply to-in those days-the governor general direct, and to no one else. That has all been changed, of course.
There was one observation made, not by the Prime Minister but by another hon. member, which should be corrected. The flag which floats on government house is the king's flag. It was settled by the king himself, and it is the flag which floats in every dominion and every union under the sovereignty of the king. It is called the king's flag because he settled the terms of it, and wherever his representative may be it is supposed to float, whether on this building, or on a building at St. John or at Halifax, or wherever it may be. In South Africa, for instance, on the one side it bears the words "The Union of South Africa" in English, and on the other side in Dutch. In this country it bears the single word "Canada," which is the same in English and in French, and there is no question of the use of different words.
That flag is a flag which was settled by the king, and is the flag which floats over the residence of the governor general, wherever he may be, whether in the capital city or some-

A Canadian Flag
*where else. But that has nothing to do with the question we are discussing to-night. It is a personal flag, given by the king to his governor general, and practically holds his power of attorney, indicating that he is the representative of the sovereign.
Is it not called the royal standard?

No, it is an entirely
different matter. The royal standard is flown only by the sovereign himself. His representative does not fly it in the dominion. It was to obviate any discussion of that character that the king's flag was settled.
I do not propose to discuss the merits or demerits of claims which may be made before a committee, but I do propose to vote for the formation of a committee. It seems to me almost monstrous that the House of Commons should deny the right of a committee to consider the advisability of our taking any step in the world. Some years ago, for instance, the hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) introduced a resolution as to how criminals should be executed, and there was a reference to a committee to consider the advisability or otherwise of the action he suggested being taken.
To-night we deal with an entirely different matter, namely the question of a flag, and the advisability of the use of it. I can quite understand the conflict of sentiment in the minds of men surveying a matter of this kind. After all, however, it does seem that we should have some method by which to identify ourselves in the eyes of those who look upon our bunting as it floats in the wind.
I visited Australia and New Zealand some months ago, and it would be a brave man indeed who would say that New Zealand was lacking in loyalty to the British crown. Yet New Zealand has a distinctive flag which it has adopted for a definite purpose. Australia, too, has a distinctive flag, and I do not think the casual observer would state that there is less devotion and loyalty to the British crown in Australia than in Canada. In fact, I think it possible that the opposite view might be taken. Those countries found -no difficulty in selecting their flags. In South Africa there was a real difficulty, and they might as well be frank to admit it. A committee was appointed, and out of the discussion in that committee there came some results. There was a good deal of acrimonious talk, but in the end there came two flags.
A very large union jack is fastened on the wall of their parliament buildings, side by side with their own flag. As has been properly pointed out before, both flags fly over the official residences, and at points where justice is administered in the different parts of the union.
There were grave difficulties to be overcome. The blacks, numbering about six million, as against two million whites, were insistent that the union jack be preserved. They had their reasons. They remembered the early days of settlement when the Boers looked upon the black men as the children of Ham, and as servants to them as lords and masters. They strongly insisted that this flag be maintained. That is the reason I take it, among others, that it finds some place, although not a very prominent one, in the flag of South Africa.
Mr. Speaker, I would be needlessly taking up the time of the house if I were to discuss. as I almost had the inclination to do, many other matters arising from this one. But the resolution before us is one for the naming of a committee for the purpose of considering the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag. To that resolution I have no difficulty in giving my assent.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that in this parliament nothing is being done for the people of Canada, I am not surprised that this should be the first motion on private members' days. After the appointment of all these committees and commissions, the House of Commons almost becomes a house of caretakers, for we have no powers or prerogatives; our functions have been usurped by commissions.
The discussion on the flag is not new, nor is the suggestion of a distinctive flag for Canada. May I point out that in the last few days twenty-eight dead soldiers have been buried by the chaplain of Christie Street hospital, their bodies bound by the union jack. That flag was good enough for 600,000 soldiers who fought for you and me in France and Flanders, and it should be good enough for the civilians who stayed at home.
This is not the time to bring forward such a motion. To-day I received twenty-five letters from housewives in Toronto who are complaining about the high cost of food and of living, and instead of talking about a new flag for Canada we might reconstitute the mass buying and spreads committee to deal with it. Many people are carrying the black flag. In my riding the people are up in arms about the high cost of living. They
A Canadian Flag

want to know what is going to be done about butter at 38 cents a pound and other necessities. We should not be considering a distinctive Canadian flag; we should be considering the black flag that is facing so many of the working classes of this country.
This resolution talks about the dominion being "an equality partner in the commonwealth of British nations." Was Canada present to-day or represented at the opening of the great dock at Singapore? New Zealand, Australia, the United States and France were there, but where was Canada,-Canada which was first in the diamond jubilee procession in the days of Sir Wilfrid Laurier who claimed to have made Canada a nation? I doubt if he would approve of the flag changes which are to be made under the auspices of this new twentieth century Liberalism which we have in this country.
If this is the most important motion to be brought up by a private member, I am willing to withdraw the resolution standing in my name so that we may get on with our business and abolish private members day. As I say, this is the third time such a resolution has been brought up since I have been in the house. In 1935, a resolution was moved by a member of the Conservative party. At one time, June, 1925, I asked certain questions about a national flag and I found out that a committee of seven civil servants had been appointed to consider the matter, all of the one religious denomination, although all good men. I believe the time is not ripe for a motion such as this.
I do not know whether Canada is in the British Empire or not. It has been contended by some of these professors in our universities and colleges and some on these commissions that Canada does not belong to the British Empire. This is what has been told to the students at McGill university and the university of Toronto, that we are a sovereign state by the Statute of Westminster. Just the other day we had quite a debate on the first reading of a bill to take away the right of appeal to the privy council. I think we have gone far enough in this direction. We should not follow the lead of South Africa and southern Ireland. The Prime Minister of South Africa has refused to take the king's oath as a privy councillor. It has been said in the House of Commons-I can give the authority-that overtures have been made to Germany and a secret treaty or agreement years ago entered into to give away part of the country covered by the Boer war treaty to Germany.

As far as I am concerned, I am utterly opposed to this motion. There is no demand for a distinctive Canadian flag. A great deal was said by these gentlemen who call themselves the Native Sons of Canada about what they were going to do to me if I opposed a new flag. However, I am still here and I do not know if there are any of them left in my riding. Your Honour will remember that when this question came up before, I asked for information from the government. My question will be found at page 4364 of Han-sand of June 17, 1925. My first question was:
Will the government lay on the table of the house the text of a copy of order in council appointing a committee to select a distinctive Canadian flag for use ashore?
Hon. members will note that I referred to use ashore. That is where our navy is most of the time, on the shore. One of the newspapers has stated that I have asked sixty-eight questions, but I only asked not sixty-eight but twelve or fourteen and half of my questions deal with the separatism which is evident in this country in our foreign affairs. I contend it is the right of a member of parliament who represents his constituents to protest in this House of Commons against the wave of separatism which has been going through this country ever since this present government came into power in 1921. We hear a lot about this celebrated Department of External Affairs. I say that the government of the day has no mandate from the people to go on the way they are going. I claim the constitutional tradition that the Minister of External Affairs shall answer in this house for the way he administers this trust. There is a possibility and a great probability that this country will be invaded before long. We have a magnificent country with wonderful resources and it is bound to be invaded and is coveted. Germany is causing considerable trouble to Britain throughout the civilized world. We hear about her opposition to communism, but she used Russia in the great war and is using her also now for her own purposes.
It is the duty of the government to inform this House of Commons what is being done by this Department of External Affairs. From three to three and a half millions of dollars have been wasted on the League of Nations and the only result has been increased disarmament by Britain. I say that this is not the time to consider such a motion. If we want to hoist a flag, let us hoist one for another mass buying and price spreads committee; let us hoist one in a fight against the high cost of living; let us hoist one in an effort to do something practical for the working classes of the country; let us hoist a

A Canadian Flag
flag on behalf of the industrial workers, fifty-one per cent of whom have been driven out of their homes through foreclosures and other measures, and want the same treatment as farmers and fishermen get. I have seen homes in my riding with the red flag of the bailiff in front showing that he had taken possession of the house and put the family on the street in executions and foreclosures.
The time has come for twentieth century Liberalism to do something practical other than a flag motion. This is not a free parliament. We might as well all go home as our work here is purely academic. There is nothing left for us to do after all these commissions have been appointed. They have taken away many of the functions and privileges of members of parliament. The people are going to protest against this motion and I doubt very much if it is in order under the Statute of Westminster. These were my questions in 1925:
2.	Who is asking for such a Canadian flag and for such a change, and why?
3.	Is the union jack not Canada's only official flag, and was it not the one used by the Canadian expeditionary forces overseas in France, and since Canada has been a British possession?
4.	Will an opportunity be given the house to discuss such an unnecessary innovation in view of Canada having no land army and no fleet whatever except the proposed Petersen fleet?
5.	Is such a change of policy not for parliament to decide instead of the governor general in council?
These are the members of the committee who were to consider these matters:
G. J. Desbarats, Esq., C.M.G., Deputy Minister of National Defence, Chairman.
Thomas Mulvey, Esq., B.A., K.C., Undersecretary of State.
A. G. Doughty, Esq., C.M.G., LL.D., Dominion Archivist.
Commodore Walter Hose, C.B.E., A.D.C., Director of the Naval Service.
Major General H. A. Panet, C.B., C.M.G., D.S.O., Adjutant General.
Group Captain J. S. Scott, M.C., A.F.C., A.D.C., Acting Director of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
That was a splendid committee, but all of one religion, it may be noted. Some were returned soldiers who had been decorated many times. But they did not want a job like that as some of them did not believe in changing the flag. Some of them had led their men in Flanders under the union jack and had seen it used many times to drape the body of some poor soldier who had been killed. No wonder the people of the motherland are wondering where Canada is going I The only thing that binds Canada to the motherland are the ties of blood and race.
Our governor general does not represent the king any more; he is just the viceroy. The
lieutenant-governors of the provinces, when they call a party together, refer to it as the viceregal party. Pick up the Globe and Mail any morning and you will see where vice-regalism has been installed in Canada illegally as the governor general is the only viceroy. As I say, there is no demand for a resolution of this type. It is all very well to talk about Canada first and the empire a very poor second.
As I have said before in the house and on many occasions outside the house the fathers of confederation made a great mistake when they foisted these provincial legislatures upon the country for political and not economic purposes. I believe in the policy of one king, one flag, one school and one empire such as the principle they have in the United States. That is a country which is copied very often to-day, and those are principles they follow there.
Saturday was Abraham Lincoln's birthday. Is anybody over there proposing to change their flag? They have one flag on the ocean, one flag on the land. Talk about a flag for the Canadian navy on the ocean! Has any part of our navy gone over to protect Canadian subjects in Japan? No; they hug the shore. When the naval bill was up in 1909 the Hon. Charles Murphy, then Secretary of State, a very respected member of this house, said that under the navy bill if an enemy ship was coming up the St. Lawrence, we would have first to pass an order in council before the Canadian navy could fire off a pinwheel, a fire cracker or a sky rocket. With a humbug navy of that kind, what is the use of saying we are a nation and all that?
I have no desire to talk out the resolution of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). I have sat on a committee with him, and I have found him very fair, and a very fair chairman. I do not want to be unfair to him or to talk out his motion, but I have been opposed to this thing for many years. The people who sent us here sent us to solve Canada's economic problems. We have been here for three and a half weeks and I fail to see any problem that we have yet solved. With conditions as they are in this country, with the many problems we have to solve, no wonder we have communism in Canada. It is the duty of this parliament to remove grievances within, because the mother country will look after grievances without. It is the armed strength of Great Britain, her navy and her army, that protect our shores, and in the old land they are beginning to wonder if Canada and the other dominions are not a drag on the British Empire.
A Canadian Flag

You had an imperial conference last year. Did you solve any of these problems there? Was this question of a Canadian flag brought up at that conference? I have not been able to find out that it was.
I want to say to these hon. gentlemen who come from the west, for whom I have every respect, that I believe in the principle of confederation, the old Cornish battle cry-" each for all and all for each." What is for the benefit of the maritimes is for the benefit of Ontario, and what is for the benefit of the great prairie provinces, which are suffering so much, is for the benefit of Ontario and the rest of Canada. We should be a happy and a united people, and this question of a change of flag should not be taken up at this time, with so many real problems before the country. We have no defence against an invader in this country, on the Pacific coast or anywhere else.
The senate have hauled down the flag on their part of the building; they have gone on a three weeks' holiday, as they have no work, they say, with all these economic problems unsolved. We have been sitting here for three weeks, and we might as well have gone on a holiday also for the last three weeks for all we have done to solve the problems of the people of Canada. If you keep on appointing commissions I do not know where you are going to end up.
Instead of having a committee appointed to consider a Canadian flag we shall soon need a pan-American flag because we are depending upon the Monroe doctrine and the American fleet to protect our shores. We are depending upon the doctrine which Monroe enunciated over a hundred years ago, and upon pan-Americanism, and if what I read about this Anglo-American treaty is correct, dear knows what kind of flag we are going to have before we get through with that treaty.
I believe in a policy of Canada for Canadians. The Toronto Star for the past few weeks has been talking about income tax of our millionaires who left Canada, and it has been printing pictures of a number of Canadian millionaires who got sick and tired of taxation under the Canadian flag and paying Canadian income tax, and went off to Nassau and other places in the Bahamas, with the wealth they got out of the gold and other mines of this country. The Lord intended all these magnificent natural resources, the water powers and mines, for all the people, not just for some of the people.
True, these people who have been engaged in mining development are entitled to a large

part of the profits, but not the whole thing uncontrolled. But they have got their millions out of the soil on easy terms, and are now in Nassau, and the flag they have there is the union jack, which is plenty good enough for us, and has been ever since we were a country. It is the flag we had in the early days of this country, in 1885, when the Grenadiers, the Queen's Own and other regiments, left the city of Toronto, the thirteenth battalion the city of Hamilton, and the sixty-fifth French-Canadian battalion from Montreal and from Quebec. These volunteers from Ontario and Quebec carried the union jack and saved Canada from being dislocated in the northwest. It was good enough for them, and it was good enough in the South African war. There was no demand for a Canadian flag then. The veterans of the South African war and the Fenian raid of 1866 are forgotten to-day. They cannot get a nickel from parliament, let alone a flag, and many of them are suffering. The same is true of the veterans of the great war. There is no demand from any soldier organization that I know of for a change of flag.
Instead of Canada doing something about a new flag, I think it had better do something about making a contribution of a unit to the British navy. It would be better to work with Australia and New Zealand, helping the British navy instead of putting up defences of our own. Let us fight our foes from within, as well as from without. This country is becoming steeped in internationalism. I do not know where it is all going to wind up. Our men will be unemployed and our home market will be gone.
Read Green's History of England; what does it say about the flag? I quoted from it in the house last year regarding the industrial revolution, and I am not going to refer to it further to-night.
As I was saying, with the toy fleet we have, I fail to see that we need a flag at all. In fact, if I went overseas to Japan, or for an ocean trip, I would not want to go to the Canadian legation for protection. I do not know whether it is open. I heard from some people over there that Canada was one of those responsible for Japan getting out of the alliance with Great Britain. Do Canadians in Japan go to the Canadian legation? I know of nobody who goes there. There is nobody there to protect them. They all head for the British embassy, the same as they do in Germany and other countries.
Next Sunday Herr Hitler is going to announce at a great demonstration, when the German flag is up. that he is going to get back Germany's colonies from Britain, if

A Canadian Flag
you please. If so, good day to the British Empire! The discussion in the house on this motion will have an unfortunate effect, I fear, in England. The mother country has made investments in Canada to protect us. She invested, and paid, for example, for the whole Rideau canal as a back door into lake Ontario. As in the war of 1812 our army was separated in Upper and Lower Canada and the Rideau canal was built to overcome this. The British paid for that, and they have made investments all over this country for defence. It is their fleet that protects our shores. We are the fifth nation in trading, and yet we have no navy. We are using the British fleet to protect our shores and our trade routes. It would be far better, Mr. Speaker, if we spent our time in trying to solve these problems of trade, defence and immigration than in talking about a flag.
I will tell the house what this Anglo-American treaty is going to do. It is going to turn the next election into a union jack election; and it is pretty nearly time we had another union jack election, to find out if we are in the empire or out of the empire and where all this separation is landing us. The government is going to have a union jack election whether it likes it or not, and motions of this kind are what will bring it along. We shall find out whether we belong in the British Empire. We are not going to follow any longer South Africa and Southern Ireland. They had an election the other day in the northern part of Ireland, and we see how the vote went.
In the last census our population was 10,352,269 people. Of these twenty-nine per cent are fine subjects of the province of Quebec, who love their native Canada and love the motherland. Another twenty-nine per cent are of foreign origin those who have come to this country. Many have been here for years; for the most part they are on the prairie; they are mostly fine people; they have done a great deal of good work out there. But they are isolationists; they do not believe in taking part in the affairs of the empire. The other forty-two per cent are the British bom, English, Irish, Scotch and Welsh. While they hate war they love Canada. The parents of many of them came here years and years ago. Though some of them may be isolationists at heart, I believe that as regards a large majority of the two twenty-nine per cents and the forty-two per cent, if the motherland were in trouble to-day their young men would spring to arms under the union jack, because the majority of the people of Canada believe that Britain before God stands as trustee the world over for the peace of the world.
In conclusion, I may say that we need not look to the newspapers to give us the facts about the foreign policy of this country. I do not know whether there is actually a censorship on foreign affairs or on defence, but it appears there must be some kind of censorship or arrangement, because in the past two years in hardly any newspapers, except the Toronto Telegram and one or two other Toronto papers and like-minded newspapers elsewhere, have I been able to find the slightest reference to foreign affairs, and the people are being kept from the real facts. The members of this house are becoming almost like what they call in England and picture in the cartoons by the name of "shiffer" sisters. That is that section of the cabinet there that would cede to Germany her colonies. If we keep on we shall be "shiffer" sisters too, because we are afraid to deal with Canada's three great problems- trade, defence and the empire, or to support rearmament.
I have consulted with a great many people about this flag issue, and the general feeling is that it would be better for us first to provide a proper fleet on which to hoist a flag, and not boats like the Minnie M, the Ada Alice, the Island Queen, the Luella, and the Shamrock. I do not know where this Canadian fleet is, though I read naval orders, and I may say that my hon. friend the minister is one for whom I have regard. I first met him out at Vancouver when he arranged to take my university of Toronto senior hockey team out in the harbour there at the time we won the Allan cup in 1927. When we went out in the harbour all we could see was the union jack.
1	have asked in the house, Where is this magnificent fleet gone to? Where is Canada's navy? I cannot remember all their names at the moment. They have gone to Barbadoes, to St. Lucia; they have gone down to Nassau, apparently. The fleet has gone junketting in foreign waters on good will cruises, away down in the West Indies. I wish some of my colleagues could go with them; I wish we could all go down there and have a good time with this Canadian navy. Naval orders of January
2	say that the fleet has gone on a good will cruise. I asked the question whether any of this celebrated fleet has gone to Sino-Japanese waters. Of course not. There might be a scrap over there, and I would not want to be on board Canada's navy when there was one there.
So I say, Mr. Speaker, so far as this particular motion is concerned, wait until we get an adequate fleet to carry a flag and sufficient men to man the fleet. On land and sea and in the air what are we doing to-day for
A Canadian Flag

our own protection? Simply hoisting the panAmerican flag in and out of this house. Apparently we are going to depend upon it now, instead of the motherland and its great flag the union jack that has so long protected our shores; instead of depending upon that any longer we are going to rely on another power on the north American continent.
We need to-day a Gilbert and Sullivan to write about this magnificent fleet of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie). We need some concert halls for a new version of Gilbert and Sullivan's H.M.S. Pinafore, as related to our toy navy. I ask again, Where is this fleet of ours which will have a change of flag if this motion passes? Where is it now? In the West Indies, down somewhere no doubt near the millionaires. I believe that one of the fleet went overseas for the Vimy Ridge celebration and another for the coronation. Nobody knows where they are at the present time. Perhaps they have on board some visitors or members or senators or others who have gone to foreign waters fur their health. It would be a good thing for the taxpayers if the members of this house could go away for three weeks also with the senate as we are doing no work for the people.
The flag in the Victorian era-that was a flag. The Victorian era built assets for the future; we have been squandering them ever since. In the days of Victoria under the union jack, the people kept the state; to-day, under the union jack, the state keeps the people. Instead of talking about a new flag, we need to-day to get the business man to hoist the union jack. Let us leave the day by day conduct of business to the men who understand and conduct business, instead of our passing a whole lot of useless motions and appointing committees and commissions of college professors to tell them how to run their business. Under the Victorian era the union jack was on top of the store in every part of Canada. Nowadays all our people are becoming proletarians; they do not own anything; they have no property. We have been slow to see how this has happened under the union jack.
Canada is becoming more and more the happy hunting ground of Americans who come to Canada seize our natural resources and then contribute nothing to the income tax. I see the young Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usiey) here to-night. Two years ago, I think it was, I asked him if he would kindly look into the way these millionaires who hoist the union jack here can go down to Nassau and escape payment and into the revelations at

Washington. He has not replied to my question. I hope he will do so this session and let us know where these people go and how they get away and no doubt hoist the union jack down there. It is a good flag, anyway. We should do well to go back to the days of Sir John A. Macdonald and remember his declaration, "A British subject I was born; a British subject I will die." I have become alarmed as I sit in the house at recent separatist developments. In the last few days we have had proposals not only to change the flag but to abolish appeals to the privy council. If those appeals are abolished, goodbye to the principles of the union jack, goodbye to the rights and privileges and functions of municipalities and the provinces, and the rights of minorities in this country. No wonder, with this wave of separatism, it is now proposed to change the flag!
The mover of the resolution states in his motion that he would have a special committee appointed. We all know what special committees are. If they are appointed they are like the royal commission, because the members of the committee just meet and sit around a table; towards the end of the session. as is known in the old country, and here, the government of the day, having a majority in the committee, will write the report for them, and the committee can vote and talk as they like and get nowhere; I have sat on many of these committees and I know what their proceedings are.
What is this committee going to consider when it is appointed? It is going to consider the advisability, if you please, of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag. Well, in my opinion, it is not advisable in the present state of unrest in the country to entertain any such distinctive proposal. In 1925, the same language was used; a committee was to consider then " the advisability of adopting a distinctive Canadian flag." Is it advisable for us to be considering a resolution such as this when we know what the condition of affairs is not only in Canada but in the world at large, when the mother country is faced with the situation that exists in the far east? Is it advisable at the present time to raise this question when we are depending upon the motherland for maritime protection?
We are trying to establish an air force in Canada. We know how war has been revolutionized in the air. If the enemy were to sail up the St. Lawrence, what would be our position? We are unprepared; while we are talking about a new flag they could blow up the citadel, proceed to Ottawa and blow

They could come here and destroy our public utilities and return in five or six hours while we were talking in a committee about the advisability of adopting a national flag. This committee is going to consider the advisability of changing our flag, but the resolution does not say the change is necessary. The new flag would no doubt please a good many people in all the provinces; but, as I say, if the enemy sailed up the St. Lawrence, where would we be? Somebody in the committee might say, "We have pan-Americanism to protect us." The resolution speaks of a Canadian flag, " representing Canada as a whole, thereby symbolizing the dominion as an equality partner in the commonwealth of British nations." I say that Canada is not an equality partner; she is a sponger partner, sponging on the taxpayers of the motherland for her maritime protection, sponging on the flag we have at the present time, the union jack, for protection not only on land but on the sea and in the air. Talk about equality partnership 1 That was the language used in the Statute of Westminster with reference to " this British Commonwealth of Nations," a high-sounding title that was supposed to bring about the millennium in empire affairs. In my opinion it has done more to disrupt the empire than anything else. The people of Canada never voted or consented to that, and they have not voted on this question with regard to a change of flag.
And what about this committee? I have sat on several committees and I can say that some of them never meet. It would be a good thing if this committee did not meet. If we are an equality partner in the commonwealth of British nations, to use the language of the resolution, all I can say is that we are making a pretty poor showing because at the present time Canada is doing nothing but the talking; Canada is doing all the talking in foreign affairs.
One of the questions before the conference had reference to shipping within the empire. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that at the present time there are 2,000 fewer merchant ships in the British Empire than there were in 1914? Do you know that this magnificent fleet which protects our shores, instead of burning coal is burning foreign petrol from Arabia and South America? If the enemy wanted to cut off our oil supply for the navy in war, we would be without a fleet to protect our shores. The fleet used to burn coal, but now burn foreign petrol. We talk about 51952-29

If we could get this house down to business we would be doing something, instead of discussing a motion of this sort. The motion speaks of a flag symbolizing the dominion. That is all we have so far as our fleet is concerned; we have the sign or symbol of a fleet; that is all. I do not know where the fleet is; I do not know what flag it flies. I think it is after eleven o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I have not concluded.
Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?
